title: Pre-Emptive Defense Against Predictable Opposition Attacks: A Methodological Framework for Single-State Policy Advocacy

detail.title: Pre-Emptive Defense Against Predictable Opposition Attacks: A Methodological Framework for Single-State Policy Advocacy
detail.abstract: This paper presents a methodological framework for the pre-emptive defense of state-level policy proposals against predictable opposition attacks. Using the Pennsylvania cannabis-legalization debate as an extended case study, the paper identifies three categories of predictable attack — the "comparator-state failure" attack (e.g., "look at California's revenue decline"), the "incumbent-industry harm" attack (e.g., "this will hurt our farmers"), and the "implementation-credibility" attack (e.g., "government cannot operationally execute this") — and develops a data-driven response architecture for each. For each attack category, the paper specifies (a) the predictable rhetorical structure, (b) the empirical record supporting or undermining the attack, (c) the optimal response framing, and (d) the conditions under which the attack will or will not succeed. The methodology generalizes beyond cannabis to any state-level policy debate in which a small number of predictable attacks consume disproportionate floor-debate time. The paper argues that pre-emptive defense — distinct from reactive rebuttal — is systematically underused in legislative communications because it requires anticipating the opposition's strongest argument before they have made it, which most advocacy organizations are structurally disinclined to do.

title: The Keystone Policy Prism II: A Game-Theoretic Analysis of Bicameral Coalition Architecture in Pennsylvania Cannabis Policy

detail.title: The Keystone Policy Prism II: A Game-Theoretic Analysis of Bicameral Coalition Architecture in Pennsylvania Cannabis Policy
detail.abstract: This paper applies non-cooperative game theory to the structural deadlock between the Pennsylvania House of Representatives (which passed HB 1200, a state-store cannabis legalization model, in May 2025 along strict party lines) and the Pennsylvania Senate (which defeated HB 1200 in committee 7–3, with Senate Law and Justice Committee Chair Dan Laughlin declaring it "dead on arrival"). The paper formalizes the deadlock as a sequential bargaining game with asymmetric committee-gatekeeper preferences and identifies the Dual-Market Bridge — a hybrid architecture combining state-controlled wholesale distribution with privately licensed retail — as the unique Nash equilibrium from which neither chamber can improve its outcome by unilaterally deviating. The analysis is structured in three parts: (I) characterization of each chamber's revealed preference structure based on roll-call data and public statements; (II) construction of the strategy space for both gatekeepers and identification of the equilibrium strategy profile; (III) sensitivity analysis showing the equilibrium's robustness to electoral-cycle perturbations and committee composition changes. The paper extends standard public-choice models of legislative bargaining by introducing a "constitutional consistency lock" — a binding-constraint mechanism by which legislators publicly committed to anti-commandeering doctrine in one policy domain (firearms) face reputational costs for opposing the same doctrine in another (cannabis). This mechanism transforms the bargaining game from a pure-coordination problem into a credibility-and-consistency problem with predictable equilibrium properties.

title: How Does Geopolitical Risk Shape Economic and Financial Outcomes in Emerging Markets? A Narrative Review
affiliations: International University of Casablanca, Business School

detail.title: How Does Geopolitical Risk Shape Economic and Financial Outcomes in Emerging Markets? A Narrative Review

declarations.declarationOfInterest: T

detail.abstract: Geopolitical risk (GPR) has become one of the defining structural forces reshaping economic and financial landscapes in the twenty-first century. Emerging market economies (EMEs) occupy a uniquely exposed position in this landscape: their institutional fragility, commodity dependence, shallower financial markets, and greater reliance on external financing amplify the transmission of geopolitical shocks relative to their advanced-economy counterparts. This narrative review synthesises 743 peer-reviewed articles published in Chartered ABS-ranked journals (Level 2 and above), drawn from a systematically assembled corpus of 2,819 records, to provide a comprehensive, critically engaged account of how GPR shapes economic and financial outcomes across emerging markets. Ten thematic clusters are identified and analysed: (1) energy markets and commodity dynamics; (2) trade flows and global supply chain disruption; (3) stock and equity market volatility; (4) macroeconomic stability and growth; (5) banking sector resilience and financial stability; (6) exchange rate and currency dynamics; (7) foreign direct investment and cross-border capital flows; (8) ESG performance and sustainable finance; (9) volatility connectedness and cross-market spillover transmission; and (10) sovereign risk and bond market dynamics. The analysis reveals several convergent findings: GPR depresses asset prices, amplifies volatility, disrupts trade, reduces investment, and deepens macroeconomic uncertainty across EMEs, with effects that are asymmetric, non-linear, and highly heterogeneous across country and institutional contexts. The review critically examines the methodological homogeneity that characterises the field (particularly the dominance of TVP-VAR connectedness frameworks) and the pronounced geographic concentration on China and Russia, which together account for 68 per cent of the corpus. The review concludes with a structured research agenda addressing the frontier questions the field has not yet adequately resolved: causal identification, micro-level evidence, institutional heterogeneity, and the distributional consequences of geopolitical risk for development.

title: The Keystone Accelerator: An Operations-Research Implementation Framework for State-Level Cannabis Market Stand-Up

detail.title: The Keystone Accelerator: An Operations-Research Implementation Framework for State-Level Cannabis Market Stand-Up
detail.abstract: This paper presents a Critical Path Method (CPM) implementation framework for the eighteen-month transition from cannabis legalization enactment to first regulated retail sale in Pennsylvania. The framework identifies the two principal critical-path bottlenecks — IT procurement (specifically, seed-to-sale tracking system deployment) and laboratory certification — and proposes parallel-processing resolutions that compress the implementation horizon by an estimated four to six months relative to baseline state-by-state experience. The paper is structured in four phases: Phase 1 (Months 0–3, Authority Formation and Emergency Rulemaking); Phase 2 (Months 4–9, Licensing Infrastructure and Lab Buildout); Phase 3 (Months 10–15, Cultivator/Processor Operational Readiness); Phase 4 (Months 16–18, Retail Launch and First Sale). For each phase, the paper specifies critical-path activities, dependency chains, resource constraints, and milestone deliverables. A stress-tested $20 million startup budget is presented with sensitivity analysis across three scenarios (baseline, conservative, accelerated). The paper also presents a transition plan for existing medical-cannabis operators that minimizes regulatory disruption while preventing incumbent monopolization. The framework is designed to be jurisdiction-portable: while the application is Pennsylvania-specific, the CPM dependency structure generalizes to any state operating from a medical-program-only baseline.

title: Exploring the intellectual capital efficiency: Measurement and impact on firm performance in the MEDA region

detail.title: Exploring the intellectual capital efficiency: Measurement and impact on firm performance in the MEDA region
detail.abstract: The study examined the relationship between intellectual capital efficiency (ICE) and firm performance across the MEDA region using the World Bank Enterprise Surveys (WBES) collected in 2019 and 2020 and estimating LSDV-regressions via OLS-models for a pooled cross-sectional dataset. Based on the resource-based view and knowledge-based theory, the empirical research adopted a conceptual approach consistent with the widely recognized value-added intellectual coefficient (VAIC) model to examine the impact of human capital efficiency (HCE), structural capital efficiency (SCE), and relational capital efficiency (RCE) on firm performance proxied by EBITDA value, and the principal component analysis (PCA) technique has been employed to obtain a consistent and unbiased value of ICE. The lack of studies on ICE in emerging and developing economies – especially with a focus on MEDA countries – makes this exploratory research noteworthy, filling a gap in the ICE literature. The findings highlight that improving knowledge-based resources can be crucial for gaining a competitive advantage in MEDA transitional economies, especially since firms with higher HCE tend to perform better. Finally, the study provides practical insights for business decision–makers and underlines the pivotal role of knowledge investments in improving firm performance.

title: Models and algorithms for the Strategic Tramp Fleet Renewal and Retrofit Problem with emission reduction -integrating tactical and operations decisions

detail.title: Models and algorithms for the Strategic Tramp Fleet Renewal and Retrofit Problem with emission reduction -integrating tactical and operations decisions

detail.abstract: We study the Strategic Tramp Fleet Renewal and Retrofit Problem (STFRRP) with emission reduction, where the fleet can be updated at regular time intervals to run on low-or zero-emission fuels by acquiring/selling/scrapping/retrofitting vessels. Since there is a strong interplay between strategic fleet renewal and tactical/operational decisions (fleet deployment and sailing speeds), the latter are also considered in the STFRRP. We propose an edge-flow and a path-flow formulation solved using two alternative algorithms, i.e., Branch-and-Price and Benders decomposition with nested Delayed-Column-Generation. We consider a real case for a deep sea dry bulk tramp shipping operator and analyze two schemes for future emission reductions, i.e., a tax-based scheme and a hard-constraint scheme. A thorough computational study is conducted to assess the models' and solution methods' efficiency. We conclude by comparing the the formulations and the solution algorithms, observing that the Benders decomposition with nested Delayed-Column-Generation is the best algorithm, especially when solving the path-flow formulation. Finally, we discuss advantages and disadvantages of the different emission reduction schemes assuming constant and increasing demand.

title: Geopolitical Risk and the Energy Transition in Emerging Market Economies: Transmission Channels, Contested Evidence, and Policy Implications
affiliations: International University of Casablanca, Business School

detail.title: Geopolitical Risk and the Energy Transition in Emerging Market Economies: Transmission Channels, Contested Evidence, and Policy Implications

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Sole author

detail.abstract: Geopolitical risk (GPR) has emerged as a structurally defining force for the global energy transition, yet its effects on emerging market economies (EMEs) remain poorly understood, methodologically contested, and geographically skewed toward a single country. This narrative review synthesises 179 studies published between 2018 and 2026, drawn from a structured Scopus search, to examine how GPR affects energy transition pathways in EMEs through four distinct but interacting transmission channels: the energy security channel, the carbon and climate nexus, the critical minerals and supply chain channel, and the green finance channel. The review advances several critical findings. First, GPR exerts a statistically robust positive effect on fossil fuel price volatility, but its second-order effect on clean energy investment is fundamentally ambiguous: energy security motives create a substitution push toward renewables, while uncertainty costs simultaneously suppress investment flows. Second, the sign of GPR on carbon emissions is genuinely contested across country contexts, with African panel studies finding emissions-increasing effects that run contrary to findings from China and OECD samples. Third, the critical minerals channel has emerged rapidly as the most policysensitive nexus, with rare earth and battery mineral supply chains now constituting strategic leverage points that shape the speed and geography of the energy transition. Fourth, green finance can buffer the uncertainty suppression mechanism, but financial market development is a precondition that most EMEs do not yet meet. Across all four channels, the literature reveals a methodological monoculture of time-series connectedness methods that establishes correlational patterns without causal identification, and a geographic monoculture heavily skewed toward China. The review concludes by proposing a research agenda oriented toward causal inference, geographic diversification, and policymechanism analysis.

detail.abstract: The proliferation of autonomous AI agents as service consumers challenges foundational assumptions in service management and platform economics. Existing frameworks-including Service-Dominant Logic and two-sided market theory-presuppose human actors as primary service beneficiaries, a condition being systematically eroded by agentic AI adoption. This paper introduces Interface Bifurcation Theory (IBT), a conceptual-typological framework classifying digital services along two dimensions: AI Consumption Intensity (ACI) and Human Visual Oversight Necessity (HVON). The resulting 2×2 typology identifies four service architectures-Traditional Visual, Supervised AI, Conversational, and Headless AI-each with distinct competitive logic and investment priorities. IBT introduces three novel constructs: Interface Value Migration, the Dual Architecture Burden, and Ecosystem Externality, and derives eight empirically testable propositions. Four illustrative cases-Bloomberg, Stripe, Epic Systems, and Perplexity AI-provide empirical grounding. Implications for service management theory, platform economics, and digital strategy are discussed.

title: Overlapping Crises Strain EU's Strategic Coherence

detail.title: Overlapping Crises Strain EU's Strategic Coherence
detail.abstract: The European Union in 2026 faces not a single dominant crisis but a convergence of overlapping pressures that simultaneously strain its decision-making capacity, fiscal resources, and political cohesion. This paper examines how Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine, renewed energy volatility linked to the Strait of Hormuz, resurgent inflation, sustained migration pressures, internal political realignment-including Hungary's post-Orbán transition-and industrial policy asymmetries interact to erode the EU's ability to convert shared strategic priorities into coordinated action. The analysis identifies three preconditions for EU coherence-shared threat assessment, sufficient fiscal and political capacity, and institutional implementation speed-and argues that all three are currently under simultaneous pressure. It further examines Germany's pivotal but constrained role as the union's primary execution power, whose hesitation or fiscal limitation produces system-wide effects. The paper concludes that the EU remains resilient but increasingly less coherent: capable of responding to individual shocks but structurally ill-equipped to absorb their compounding interaction before the next disruption arrives.

title: Sociotechnical Challenges of Defence AI: Automation Bias, Human Control and Accountability

detail.title: Sociotechnical Challenges of Defence AI: Automation Bias, Human Control and Accountability

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve real human participants or real-world data collection. The dataset used is synthetically generated to simulate experimental conditions. Therefore, formal ethics approval and informed consent were not required.

detail.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into defence operations promises enhanced situational awareness and faster decision-making, yet it also introduces sociotechnical challenges relating to human autonomy, accountability and bias. Recent policy documents warn that AI can alter cognitive skills, shape preferences and induce automation bias, leading operators to accept erroneous suggestions [1], [2]. Human-machine teaming is increasingly seen as the default configuration in military AI [3], but empirical evidence on how AI decision support systems (DSS) affect human performance remains limited. This study empirically examines automation bias in a simulated targeting task. Sixty participants performed target identification under three conditions: manual control, low-autonomy AI DSS and high-autonomy AI DSS. Half of the participants received interface transparency and bias-mitigation training. Measures included misidentification rates, response times and trust. Results show that high autonomy AI DSS increased misidentification rates by 150% compared with manual control, while transparency and training reduced these errors by 40%. Participants using transparent AI systems displayed lower unwarranted trust, faster correction of AI errors and better situational awareness. These findings suggest that socio-technical design choices and training can mitigate automation bias and support meaningful human control. The study contributes empirical evidence to debates on responsible military AI and offers practical recommendations for defence organisations developing AI-enabled systems.

title: Same Risk, New Wrapper: Contagion Between Traditional and Tokenized Private Credit

detail.title: Same Risk, New Wrapper: Contagion Between Traditional and Tokenized Private Credit
detail.abstract: The global private credit market has grown to nearly $2 trillion in assets under management, drawing capital from pension funds, endowments, and retail investors seeking yields unavailable in traditional fixed income markets. The first quarter of 2026 marked the sector's first serious stress test since the post-2008 expansion, as redemption waves swept through major private credit vehicles and JPMorgan Chase initiated targeted valuation markdowns on software loans it deemed vulnerable to artificial intelligence disruption. This paper examines those events and their implications for tokenized private credit, a parallel market in which blockchain-based protocols offer on-chain exposure to similar underlying loans. Using Maple Finance's syrupUSDC yield token and SYRUP governance token as primary case studies, the analysis evaluates how credit deterioration in traditional lending markets transmits to decentralized finance platforms. The paper argues that tokenization improves transparency but does not alter the fundamental economics of private lending: borrower default risk, liquidity mismatches, leverage amplification, and sector concentration follow the asset class regardless of its technological wrapper. For policymakers, the emergence of tokenized real-world assets represents a new channel through which credit cycle stress can reach a broader and less sophisticated investor base.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the Cognitive Attractor Capacity (CAC) framework and its operational mechanism, the Constitutional Contestability Loop (CCL), as a systems-level model for understanding how constitutional architecture conditions long-run cognitive performance. It advances a structural theory of constitutional function by reframing the relationship between governance, innovation, and sustained system performance.

The paper argues that cross-national differences in innovation outcomes—particularly the concentration of breakthrough achievement, the persistence of talent inflows, and the capacity for adaptive renewal—are not adequately explained by material variables such as geography, capital, or population. Instead, these differences reflect variation in institutional conditions, specifically the extent to which systems preserve contestability, enable information flow, and sustain error correction over time.

CAC is defined as the capacity of institutional environments to attract, integrate, and amplify globally distributed cognitive inputs. This capacity is operationalized through the CCL, a closed-loop dynamic in which contestability enables error detection, error detection produces innovation, innovation attracts talent, and talent inflows expand variation, which is integrated through alignment and coherence. Together, CAC and CCL explain how constitutional systems convert dispersed knowledge into sustained innovation and renewal.

Drawing on empirical patterns—including Nobel-level achievement concentration, divergence between innovation throughput and breakthrough discovery, variation in educational structures, and long-run migration flows—the paper demonstrates that systems with comparable resources produce materially different outcomes consistent with differences in institutional architecture. Comparative analysis further shows that systems can sustain high output under centralized coordination, but exhibit reduced capacity for non-incremental innovation where contestability is constrained.

The analysis identifies a central diagnostic error—the causality reversal problem—whereby outputs such as wealth and productivity are treated as drivers rather than lagging indicators of underlying institutional processes. This misinterpretation obscures structural degradation, which often proceeds informally through the narrowing of discourse, incentive distortion, and the substitution of speed or consensus for adversarial evaluation.

The Constitution is therefore reconceptualized as renewable cognitive infrastructure: a system governing information flow, error correction, and institutional legitimacy. Innovation emerges as a consequence of preserved contestability, not as a direct policy objective.

The paper concludes that the modern frontier is no longer geographic, but institutional. Long-run performance depends on whether systems preserve the conditions necessary to generate, test, and refine ideas over time. The Constitution, in this sense, functions as the boundary of renewal—determining whether a system can continue to adapt and correct itself across generations.

title: DMCC Compliance as a Source of Rising Regulatory Costs

detail.title: DMCC Compliance as a Source of Rising Regulatory Costs

detail.abstract:
The Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act (DMCC) marks a structural turning point in the United Kingdom’s approach to governing digital markets. Whereas traditional competition law relies on retrospective, evidence-driven and case-specific enforcement, the DMCC establishes an ex-ante regulatory architecture centered on the designation of firms with Strategic Market Status (SMS), the imposition of tailor-made conduct requirements, and ongoing supervisory intervention by the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA).

UK policymakers justified this regime shift by arguing that conventional antitrust enforcement is too slow and too reactive to address the structural risks allegedly associated with large digital platforms. In this view, information asymmetries, rapid innovation cycles and high switching costs would justify a framework that disciplines firms before competitive harm materializes. The DMCC is therefore presented as a more agile institutional solution: faster because it anticipates intervention; more predictable because obligations apply to firms designated under pre-set criteria; and more effective because it equips the CMA with extensive investigative and remedial powers, including the ability to impose conduct requirements and, ultimately, structural remedies.

But replacing contextual, effect-based analysis with a system of firm-specific mandates is neither economically neutral nor legally trivial. The DMCC creates broad, intrusive and technically complex obligations that require significant reengineering of products, internal processes, and business models. These obligations apply even in the absence of demonstrated competitive harm – the mere fact of SMS designation is sufficient to trigger extensive duties related to fairness, openness, interoperability, data access, discrimination controls and transparency. While the DMCC includes provisions requiring the CMA to demonstrate that the imposition of a conduct requirement is proportional and expected to benefit consumers, the breadth and indeterminacy of these obligations introduce substantial compliance burdens and uncertainty, particularly because the CMA retains wide discretion in how it interprets, implements and updates conduct requirements over time.

The institutional architecture of the DMCC further amplifies these frictions. Its designation process combines qualitative assessments (such as "substantial and entrenched market power" and "strategic significance") with flexible quantitative indicators, allowing wide interpretative latitude. Its supervisory mechanisms include continuous monitoring, compulsory information requests, and the controversial ability to intervene directly in product design or data architectures, even compelling firms to generate information by varying their usual conduct or running specific tests. The CMA’s toolkit, including enforcement notices and structural interventions, sets a high-stakes regulatory environment in which the nature of appeals is asymmetric: while CMA decisions to impose financial penalties are subject to a full merits review, most substantive decisions, such as SMS designation or intervention imposition, can only be challenged through the limited Judicial Review standard.

Within this context, this study argues that – despite its promise of greater efficiency and foresight – the DMCC generates two cumulative layers of regulatory cost even before any evidence of anticompetitive conduct is established. First, direct costs, arising from the need to reconfigure products and systems, adapt internal workflows to new transparency, data and interoperability duties, and respond to extensive CMA information-gathering and compliance processes. Second, indirect costs, embedded in the DMCC’s structural features: regulatory uncertainty, wide CMA discretion, procedural volatility, and the chilling effects these conditions have on investment, innovation and the capacity to compete dynamically – especially in markets characterized by high sunk costs and rapid technological evolution.

title: When Crypto Meets Credit: Empirical Evidence on SYRUP Governance Token Return Dynamics

detail.title: When Crypto Meets Credit: Empirical Evidence on SYRUP Governance Token Return Dynamics
detail.abstract: The global private credit market has grown to nearly $2 trillion in assets under management, drawing capital from pension funds, endowments, and retail investors seeking yields unavailable in traditional fixed income markets. The first quarter of 2026 marked the sector's first serious stress test since the post-2008 expansion, as redemption waves swept through major private credit vehicles and JPMorgan Chase initiated targeted valuation markdowns on software loans it deemed vulnerable to artificial intelligence disruption. This paper examines those events and their implications for tokenized private credit, a parallel market in which blockchain-based protocols offer on-chain exposure to similar underlying loans. Using Maple Finance's syrupUSDC yield token and SYRUP governance token as primary case studies, the analysis evaluates how credit deterioration in traditional lending markets transmits to decentralized finance platforms. The paper argues that tokenization improves transparency but does not alter the fundamental economics of private lending: borrower default risk, liquidity mismatches, leverage amplification, and sector concentration follow the asset class regardless of its technological wrapper. For policymakers, the emergence of tokenized real-world assets represents a new channel through which credit cycle stress can reach a broader and less sophisticated investor base.

title: Private Credit Stress and Tokenized Lending: Contagion Risks Between Traditional Funds and Blockchain-Based Credit Markets

detail.title: Private Credit Stress and Tokenized Lending: Contagion Risks Between Traditional Funds and Blockchain-Based Credit Markets
detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of private credit markets over the past decade has reshaped the structure of corporate lending and created a large parallel credit system operating outside traditional banking institutions. At the same time, developments in blockchain technology have enabled decentralized finance platforms to tokenize real-world credit assets, allowing investors to gain exposure to lending pools through digital tokens. These developments raise important questions about whether tokenization meaningfully changes the economic risks associated with private lending or simply redistributes traditional credit exposures through new technological infrastructure. This paper examines emerging signs of stress in the private credit market during 2025 and 2026 and evaluates whether these developments may transmit to decentralized finance lending platforms that provide exposure to tokenized credit assets. Drawing on literature related to shadow banking, liquidity risk, financial contagion, and decentralized finance, the analysis explores structural similarities between traditional private credit funds and blockchain-based lending pools. The findings suggest that although tokenization can improve transparency and settlement efficiency, it does not eliminate the fundamental credit risks associated with illiquid lending markets. Borrower default risk, leverage, sector concentration, and macroeconomic cycles continue to shape outcomes in both traditional and tokenized credit markets.

title: Self-Preferencing in the Competitive Dynamics of Platform Markets

detail.title: Self-Preferencing in the Competitive Dynamics of Platform Markets

declarations.funderStatement: This paper was prepared with support from Facebook Brasil.

detail.abstract:
The rise of digital platforms has prompted a fundamental reassessment of competition law, leading to the emergence of ex ante regulatory frameworks such as the European Union’s Digital Markets Act and the United Kingdom’s Digital Markets, Competition and Consumer Act. These regimes depart from traditional ex post enforcement by imposing predefined obligations on firms designated as gatekeepers, based on the assumption that certain practices are inherently anticompetitive when conducted by dominant platforms. Among these, self-preferencing has become a central concern, grounded in the belief that it distorts competition, leverages data-driven advantages, and entrenches irreversible market power through network effects.

This paper challenges the analytical foundations of such ex ante prohibitions. It argues that the prevailing regulatory approach relies on static, industrial-era metrics that inadequately capture the dynamics of digital markets. First, practices such as vertical integration, cross-subsidization, and network effects are intrinsic to platform business models and may generate efficiencies rather than exclusion. Second, large datasets and extensive user bases do not necessarily confer insurmountable market power, as factors such as multi-homing and the non-exclusive nature of data enhance market contestability. Third, network effects operate as double-edged mechanisms, capable of both reinforcing and undermining incumbency in response to shifts in user behavior and innovation.

By reassessing the role of scale, data, and integration in digital ecosystems, the paper contends that self-preferencing should not be presumed anticompetitive. Instead, it may function as a legitimate strategy to enhance efficiency, coordination, and innovation. The findings call for a more nuanced, effects-based approach to competition enforcement that reflects the dynamic and evolving nature of digital markets

detail.abstract: Organizations increasingly rely on artificial intelligence capabilities that are externally supplied, embedded in vendor platforms, or otherwise outside their full operational control. When such capabilities sit inside critical workflows, disruption risk extends beyond model performance or governance concerns and becomes a business continuity and resilience problem. A workflow-centered framework is proposed to analyze this form of dependence by linking AI supply-chain exposure, third-party assurance concerns, and continuity design. The framework distinguishes key dependency types and disruption modes and organizes continuity planning around dependency mapping, fallback design, switching readiness, monitoring triggers, resilience testing, and recovery logic. detail.abstract: Comparing the technical efficiency of firms that operate under different production technologies requires a metafrontier framework that envelops group-specific frontiers. Despite a substantial methodological literature and growing applied demand, no comprehensive R package for metafrontier analysis has been available on CRAN. We introduce metafrontier, a package that provides a unified interface for three complementary approaches: the deterministic metafrontier of Battese, Rao, and O'Donnell (2004), the stochastic metafrontier of Huang, Huang, and Liu (2014), and DEA-based metafrontier models. The package estimates groupspecific frontiers, constructs the metafrontier envelope, and decomposes efficiency into group technical efficiency and the technology gap ratio. Additional features include the metafrontier Malmquist productivity index with three-way decomposition, bootstrap confidence intervals for technology gap ratios, Murphy-Topel corrected standard errors, latent class metafrontier estimation via the EM algorithm, panel stochastic frontier models with time-varying inefficiency, and ggplot2 visualisation methods. An interoperability layer accepts pre-fitted models from sfaR, frontier, and Benchmarking. We illustrate the package with simulated examples and a Monte Carlo study demonstrating parameter recovery under both metafrontier estimators. All examples and simulations are fully reproducible and complete in under ten minutes on a standard laptop.

title: Simple Policies for Serial Inventory Systems with Lost Sales: Beyond the Echelon Base-Stock Policy
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK)

detail.title: Simple Policies for Serial Inventory Systems with Lost Sales: Beyond the Echelon Base-Stock Policy
detail.abstract: We study a classical periodic-review serial inventory system with lost sales. While the echelon base-stock (EBS) policy is optimal under backlogging, it is generally suboptimal and can perform poorly in lost-sales environments. Moreover, computing optimal policies for multistage systems becomes intractable due to the curse of dimensionality. To address these challenges, we propose two new classes of heuristic replenishment policies: the echelon projected non-stockout probability (EPP3) policy and the echelon projected inventory level (EPIL) policy. We first develop single-index versions of both policies and show that they are asymptotically optimal as unit penalty costs grow large. To enhance performance, we further introduce sequentially optimized and dual-index variants and derive performance bounds for dual-index EPIL policies when external replenishment lead times are large. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed policies consistently achieve near-optimal performance and substantially outperform the EBS policy. Finally, we extend our framework to assembly inventory systems with lost sales by introducing balanced EPP3 and EPIL policies and show that all asymptotic results established for serial systems carry over to assembly systems.

detail.abstract: The "Institute Management System" (IMS) is a full-stack web application designed to digitize and streamline the day-today administrative operations of educational institutes. A significant barrier to efficient institute administration is data fragmentationstudent records, course catalogs, and public inquiries scattered across spreadsheets, paper files, and email threads. This thesis presents the design and implementation of a centralized digital management platform built using Angular 17 (frontend) and Spring Boot 3 with Java 21 (backend), communicating via a RESTful API over HTTP/JSON. The system implements full CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) operations for three core entities-Courses, Students, and Messages-and exposes a real-time administrative dashboard alongside a public-facing website for prospective students. The backend employs Spring Data JPA with an H2 in-memory database, while the frontend uses Angular Material Design components, Reactive Forms with dual-layer validation, and lazy-loaded modules for performance optimization. A comprehensive 3-tier architecture-Presentation, Business Logic, and Data layersensures clean separation of concerns and extensibility. Functional testing across 15 test scenarios yielded a 100% pass rate; Lighthouse performance metrics recorded a First Contentful Paint of under 0.5 seconds and API response times below 50 ms. This work demonstrates that modern full-stack technologies, applied with disciplined architectural thinking, deliver scalable, maintainable, and user-friendly solutions to real-world educational management challenges.

title: Canadian Textile Waste as a Market Failure: Cost Externalization and Global Trade Dynamics

detail.title: Canadian Textile Waste as a Market Failure: Cost Externalization and Global Trade Dynamics
detail.abstract:
The rapid expansion of the global fashion industry has led to a significant increase in

textile waste, raising critical environmental and economic concerns. This study examines the

inefficiencies of textile waste management through an economic lens, focusing on Canada and

its connection to global second-hand clothing flows. While circular economy solutions such as

recycling are gaining attention, their adoption remains limited due to high costs and structural

constraints. At the same time, large volumes of textile waste are exported to African countries,

where a substantial share becomes an environmental burden rather than reuse. Drawing on

interviews with industry experts and recent data, this paper explores how current systems

create economic distortions and unequal outcomes. The findings highlight the need for better

policy alignment, improved infrastructure, and stronger incentives to support a more

sustainable and transparent textile economy.

title: When Integration Fails: Collusion and Risk Sharing in Renewable Electricity Markets
affiliations: Kyoto University, University of Hyogo and University of Hyogo

detail.title: When Integration Fails: Collusion and Risk Sharing in Renewable Electricity Markets
detail.abstract: Market integration plays a central role in allowing renewable electricity systems to manage supply variability through spatial risk sharing. Yet integration can strengthen incentives for large utilities to restrict interregional trade to preserve local market power. We study how a cartel among Japanese utilities reduced interregional transmission and weakened market integration. We show that reduced transmission increased reliance on local balancing through pumped hydro storage, yet solar curtailment risk increased in renewable-rich regions. These results show how distortions to cross-regional trade can propagate through system adjustment, weakening the ability of electricity markets to absorb renewable surpluses. More broadly, our findings highlight a central economic insight: while storage helps manage temporal fluctuations in renewable supply, it cannot fully substitute for the spatial risk-sharing function of transmission. Transmission and storage instead play distinct but supplemental roles in renewable electricity markets.

title: A Countercyclical Capital Buffer for Reinsurance; Evidence from the Underwriting Cycle, 1990-2024

detail.title: A Countercyclical Capital Buffer for Reinsurance; Evidence from the Underwriting Cycle, 1990-2024
detail.abstract: Current reinsurance solvency frameworks are structurally procyclical, permitting reserve depletion when systemic fragility accumulates. This paper develops a Composite Cycle Indicator (CCI) and countercyclical capital buffer extending the Basel III macroprudential logic to reinsurance. The CCI combines four HP-filtered components-rate-on-line gap, capital surplus, combined-ratio gap, and risk-adjusted spread compression. A piecewiselinear activation rule links the CCI to a surcharge on the Solvency Capital Requirement. The analytical framework draws on convention-driven pricing under fundamental uncertainty, generating Minskyan dynamics in which the market migrates from hedge to speculative to Ponzi positions. The paper sets out a three-year shadow-run implementation roadmap under which retrospective calibration, bootstrap inference, Hamilton-filter robustness checks, Markov analysis of phase transitions, and agent-based equilibrium simulation would be executed by the macroprudential authority before binding activation.

detail.abstract: We use novel Medicare data that link spouses to examine how one spouse's sudden incapacitation affects their partner's need for formal care. A spouse's health shock causes their partner to be 18% more likely to visit a skilled nursing facility. That pattern reflects both a change in health and a shift from informal care to formal care. After one spouse is incapacitated, the other spouse becomes less sensitive to the price of formal care. We explore the implications for optimal health insurance contracts, showing these within-household spillovers imply that the optimal health insurance contract should provide more generous coverage to those whose spouses are incapacitated relative to those whose spouses are available to provide care.

detail.abstract: Bangladesh's government AI readiness rank improved from 82nd 2023) to 75th 2025) on the Oxford Insights Government AI Readiness Index, suggesting meaningful national progress. Yet during this same period, the country operated without a functional national AI council, lacked a gazetted national AI policy, maintained research expenditure at 0.3% of GDP, and recorded a 22% accuracy drop for rural dialect inputs in government-deployed AI systems BRAC Institute of Governance and Development BIGD , 2024. This paper critically examines the divergence between improving index scores and stagnating implementation capacity-a phenomenon defined here as the AI Readiness Paradox. Triangulating three independent global indices-Oxford Insights 2024 , the Network Readiness Index NRI; Portulans Institute, 2024 , and the Centre for the Governance of AI Algorithmic Accountability Index 2025 the study demonstrates convergent structural weakness across governance, infrastructure, and human capital dimensions. Despite employing distinct methodologies and indicator sets, all three indices identify the same pattern of surface-level readiness masking deep implementation deficits. Drawing on Socio-Technical Systems Theory Trist & Bamforth, 1951 , the paper proposes a dual-metric framework distinguishing Index Readiness Score IRS) from Implementation Capacity Score ICS. Applied to Bangladesh and four comparator countries, the framework reveals that Bangladesh exhibits the largest IRS ICS gap: an IRS of 46.01/100 alongside an ICS of 37.5/100-the only country in the sample where the index overestimates implementation capacity. This study provides the first systematic quantitative critique of AI readiness index methodology for Bangladesh and offers five evidence-based policy recommendations for closing the implementation gap in developing economies.

title: Household Balance Sheets and Spatial Polarization: A Dynamic Spatial Incomplete Markets Model with Endogenous Sorting

detail.title: Household Balance Sheets and Spatial Polarization: A Dynamic Spatial Incomplete Markets Model with Endogenous Sorting
detail.abstract: This paper develops a lifecycle spatial incomplete-markets model with endogenous migration and housing to study the aggregate and distributional consequences of spatial polarization. The model emphasizes a resource-composition channel: migration incentives depend on the relative importance of location-dependent labor income versus location-independent asset returns over the lifecycle. Calibrated to South Korea as a bounding case of extreme polarization, the model predicts that young, asset-poor households sort into the high-wage, high-rent capital region, while asset-rich households have weaker incentives to relocate. In the stationary equilibrium, this mechanism leaves 41.5% of high-productivity workers in the periphery and generates a labor-income loss equal to 3.6% of GDP. Counterfactuals yield three main results. First, weakening agglomeration forces reduces spatial inequality but at a substantial output cost. Second, increasing housing supply elasticity in the capital lowers rents on impact but ultimately raises population concentration through endogenous migration and agglomeration. Third, removing migration frictions lowers aggregate GDP by 2.0% and reduces consumption-based welfare by 1.5%, with larger losses for asset-poor households because they are more exposed to the general-equilibrium wage decline.

title: Does the Peter Principle Apply to Paula? Incentive Responsiveness and Promotion Decisions in Financial Institutions
affiliations: Southern Methodist University (SMU) - Finance Department, Southern Methodist University (SMU) - Finance Department and Southern Methodist University (SMU) - SMU Cox School of Business

detail.title: Does the Peter Principle Apply to Paula? Incentive Responsiveness and Promotion Decisions in Financial Institutions
detail.abstract: Firms face a costly trade-off in promotion decisions: reward top performers to motivate effort or select those with the highest expected managerial performance. Exploiting mandatory disclosure requirements in the U.S. mortgage industry, we test whether firms mitigate these costs by placing greater weight on managerial fit for workers who respond less strongly to promotion incentives. A natural source of such heterogeneity is gender. Prior research suggests women are more likely to exhibit traits such as greater risk aversion and lower competitiveness, which moral hazard models predict dampen effort responses to promotion-based incentives. Among 88,000 loan officers at approximately 1,000 firms, we find that firms' promotion decisions favor current sales performance over managerial fit for male workers, consistent with the Peter Principle. In contrast, firms place greater weight on managerial fit for female workers, mitigating the Peter Principle mismatch costs. We also provide direct evidence on the mechanism that promotion incentives are less consequential for women's behavior than for men's: female loan officers reduce effort less than male loan officers after being passed over for promotion to manager, increase effort less when managerial openings arise, and are less likely to leave the industry following high performance. Our results show that firms mitigate the incentive-fit conflict in promotions in a manner consistent with economic theory.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Rossiter Method (RM), a systematic monthly allocation rule for portfolios of Brazilian real estate investment funds (FIIs). RM combines a target-price operator T , which fuses volatility-adaptive Bollinger bands, quantile-based local supports, and a quality factor from dividend yield and price-to-book, with a two-phase allocation operator A that translates monthly contributions into good-till-cancelled limit orders (Phase 1) with a market-price fallback (Phase 2). Across four backtests spanning November 2019 to March 2026, RM delivers higher terminal wealth, higher time-weighted returns, lower drawdowns, and superior differential Sharpe ratios compared with naïve dollar-cost averaging (DCA), while preserving full monthly investment of contributions and avoiding taxable rebalancing events. title: Accounting Reports, Macro News, and Higher-Order Beliefs

detail.title: Accounting Reports, Macro News, and Higher-Order Beliefs
detail.abstract: This paper develops a model of financial markets with higher-order beliefs to study how accounting information affects investor coordination and market efficiency. Investors observe a public macroeconomic signal, a firm-level accounting report, and private signals about a common fundamental. The accounting report is semi-public: it can be strategically biased by the manager, is subject to measurement noise (report precision), and is interpreted heterogeneously by investors (interpretation clarity). We show that report precision and interpretation clarity play distinct roles: precision improves learning about fundamentals, while clarity strengthens coordination by aligning investors' interpretations. As a result, coordination can either discipline or amplify reporting bias. Improving report precision is welfare-enhancing when the macroeconomic signal is sufficiently informative: by curbing excess coordination on macro news, higher accounting precision redirects reliance toward more informative firm-level information. The socially optimal accounting precision first increases and then decreases with the quality of macroeconomic signals. When macro news is poor, a more precise accounting report provides the greatest welfare gain by alleviating excess coordination on a noisy anchor.

title: International Accounting Harmonization and Global Supply Chain Stability
affiliations: Lancaster University - Lancaster University Management School, University of Tennessee, Haslam College of Business, Accounting and Information Management and Beijing Jiaotong University

detail.title: International Accounting Harmonization and Global Supply Chain Stability

detail.abstract: Drawing on relational contract theory, we argue that harmonization of domestic accounting standards with International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) enhances financial statement comparability and transparency, thereby weakening firms' relational contracts with foreign suppliers and increasing the likelihood of foreign supplier relationship terminations. Using a stacked difference-indifferences design and a global sample of 1,273 manufacturing firms across 34 jurisdictions, we find that firms adopting or converging with IFRS terminate more relationships with their foreign suppliers in the two years following harmonization than before its implementation. This effect is more pronounced when information asymmetries between firms and their foreign suppliers are more substantially reduced, when their relational contracts were weaker, and when they previously exhibited greater reliance on relational contracting. We also observe that although stronger firms are able to reconfigure their supply chains and benefit from new transactional partnerships, weaker firms struggle to attract new suppliers and experience future declines in profitability, stock returns, and trade credit. Overall, our study offers novel insights into how accounting harmonization reshapes the dynamics of global trade. Our findings advance the literature by applying relational contract theory to the IFRS context and by documenting international supply chain instability as an unintended consequence of international accounting harmonization.

detail.title: Reflexive Simplification: The Governance of Clarity

detail.abstract: This article compares how the European Union, the United States, and the United Kingdom pursue regulatory simplification in financial regulation, and argues that prevailing accounts mischaracterize simplification as reduction, whereas in practice it operates as a reflexive governance technique. It shows that 'simplification' should not be understood merely as the reduction of rules or the rationalization of drafting, but as an institutional practice through which regulatory systems seek to make complexity intelligible, revisable, and governable. The study demonstrates that these regulatory traditions organize clarity through distinct legal technologies: layered codification in the EU, procedural iteration and retrospective review in the United States, and regulator-led rulebook restructuring in the United Kingdom. Building on this comparison, the article develops the concept of reflexive simplification as a framework for analyzing how efforts to produce clarity redistribute authority, reshape expert knowledge, and alter compliance burdens. It then applies this framework to sustainable finance, comparing the EU's SFDR-CSRD-Taxonomy nexus with parallel UK and US disclosure trajectories. Its central claim is that, across regulatory traditions, simplification increasingly works through complexity rather than against it. What varies across systems is not the underlying problem, but the institutional form through which clarity is produced.

detail.abstract: Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) remains a foundational instrument of environmental governance, designed to evaluate the environmental implications of development projects prior to approval. However, in many emerging economies, EIA frameworks continue to operate within static analytical boundaries, insufficiently accounting for climate-related risks despite increasing exposure to extreme weather events, sea-level rise, and long-term climatic variability. This limitation constrains the ability of EIA to function as an effective forward-looking decision-support tool. This paper demonstrates that the limited integration of climate risk within conventional EIA frameworks represents a structural gap in environmental governance. Drawing on a critical review of EIA regulations, climate risk assessment literature, and sustainability governance practices, the study identifies key deficiencies, including reliance on historical baseline conditions, limited incorporation of future climate scenarios, and weak treatment of cumulative and long-term risks. To address these challenges, the paper advances the Dynamic Climate-Responsive EIA (DCR-EIA) Framework, a structured approach that embeds climate risk considerations across all stages of the assessment process. The framework emphasises climate-sensitive baseline analysis, scenario-based impact evaluation, and adaptive mitigation planning, translating climate risk into actionable insights for project appraisal and regulatory decision-making. By repositioning EIA as a climate-responsive governance instrument, the study contributes to ongoing environmental assessment reform while offering practical relevance for environmental consulting and sustainability practice in emerging economies.

detail.abstract:
• Artificial intelligence has renewed optimism about improving Canada’s long-standing productivity problem, but history shows that general-purpose technologies often take decades to produce measurable economy-wide gains. Early adoption typically produces modest improvements as firms experiment and invest in complementary assets such as data, skills, and organizational changes.
  • Canada performs reasonably well in international AI rankings and produces strong research output, but it lags leading countries in computing capacity and commercialization. Canadians are among the most frequent users of generative AI tools globally, yet business adoption remains uneven and relatively limited.
  • Canadian data show that about 12 percent of businesses currently use AI, and most report little change in employment following adoption. Many firms say AI is not relevant to their operations or lack the knowledge needed to implement it effectively, suggesting adoption barriers remain significant.
  • Policy should therefore prioritize accelerating AI adoption and diffusion across sectors while maintaining Canada’s research and infrastructure capacity. Governments can support this by improving regulatory clarity, expanding data access, strengthening AI literacy, and encouraging firms to experiment and integrate AI into their operations.

title: Keeping Strategic Futures Observable in AI Strategy: Counterfactual Observability and Evidence Architecture under Radical Uncertainty

detail.title: Keeping Strategic Futures Observable in AI Strategy: Counterfactual Observability and Evidence Architecture under Radical Uncertainty
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is not only being used strategically but as a recurring infrastructure to generate, compare, monitor, and refine alternatives in strategy. Research has shown that AI can broaden attention, speed feedback, improve strategic reasoning, support analogies, and enable some types of foresight. However, there are many other risks associated with the use of AI in strategy. For example, after one future enters execution, AI-enabled strategy systems have the capability to redistribute evidence toward the enacted path and away from serious non-enacted futures. I define this risk as the counterfactual observability gap the widening difference in the rate, richness, and review visibility of decision-relevant evidence generated for an enacted future compared to a serious shadow future after provisional commitment. The gap depletes the strategic futures reserve available at any point in time, defined as the stock of alternatives that remain legible, legitimate, and practically reversible under radical uncertainty. My central claim is that AI-enabled strategy can fail by recommending the wrong path ex ante, or by changing how evidence is collected, organized, and presented ex post so that rival paths become evidentially silent before uncertainty has materially receded. I develop a formalized theoretical model in which AI increases the velocity of evidence produced for the enacted path while survival of shadow futures depends upon proxy evidence, sponsorship, and retained capability for re-entry. I then specify counterfactual evidence architecture as a governance response: separable comparison dashboards, bounded probes, anomaly-triggered re-estimation, shadow sponsorship, reserve budgets, modular capability retention, and dual cadence. The article contributes to AI and strategy, real options, attention-based theory, path dependence, strategy-as-practice, and AI epistemic-regime research by shifting the dependent variable from option generation to option survival. It concludes with falsifiable hypotheses, a flagship randomized experiment, archival event-history tests, construct measures, public-case illustrations, and a managerial protocol for less self-erasing strategy systems.

title: Rethinking Healthcare Service Resilience: A Critical Review and Development of a QuantitativeResilience Framework
affiliations: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Imperial College London

detail.title: Rethinking Healthcare Service Resilience: A Critical Review and Development of a QuantitativeResilience Framework
detail.abstract: Mismanaging a healthcare institution's operations in the face of adverse events can lead not only to financial losses but also to patient neglect, higher casualty rates, and personnel burnout. To evaluate a healthcare institution's capacity to withstand adverse events, managers assess its resilience quantitatively. Healthcare service resilience is the healthcare institution's capacity to prepare for, resist, absorb, and recover quickly from adverse events affecting its services. However, extant quantitative frameworks fail to capture the complexity of healthcare service resilience, leading to limited contextual applicability and operational guidance. To better understand this complexity, we propose a set of formal properties for healthcare service resilience. A critical review of 30 quantitative resilience frameworks revealed that none fulfills all properties simultaneously, potentially compromising patient care. Therefore, we introduce a novel healthcare service resilience framework that enables consistent comparison across healthcare institutions and adverse events.Our framework offers an integrated overview of complex healthcare operations, highlighting both the operational and clinical impacts of adverse events. To demonstrate the managerial value of our framework, we present a real-world case study focusing on a surgical ward within a Taiwanese hospital in response to a mass casualty incident involving over 200 patients. For instance, switching to a policy favored by our framework results in a 64% increase in satisfied demand, a 5% improvement in quality of care, a 12% reduction in recovery time, and a 41% increase in resilience.

detail.abstract:
The 2030 Agenda's seventeen Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) represent an unprecedented global consensus, yet nearly a decade into implementation, structural fragmentation, voluntary compliance, and metric myopia have rendered them insufficient for addressing compound planetary crises. This paper interrogates the governance architecture required to transition from aspirational goal-setting to systemic execution. 
Drawing on UN institutional frameworks, localization data, and mission-oriented policy theory, we propose the Nexus for Systems Missions (N4SM) framework as a nextgeneration coordination platform. N4SM collapses siloed targets into six integrated missions, embeds planetary boundaries and well-being metrics, operationalizes whole-ofgovernment and whole-of-society approaches through open digital infrastructure, and introduces binding accountability mechanisms. 
The paper outlines a design-science methodology, presents anticipated contributions to global governance innovation, and engages contrarian critiques regarding technocratic centralization, digital divides, and sovereignty constraints. Strategic recommendations for phased institutionalization, metric transition, and South-South cooperation are advanced to rewire global sustainability governance from performative compliance to collective, accountable stewardship.

affiliations: University College London, University College London, University College London, University College London, University College London, University College London, University College London, University College London, Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children NHS Foundation Trust, Imperial College London - Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust and University College London - University College London Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust

detail.title: Patients’ and carers’ interests and behaviours related to the sustainability of medicines: A qualitative study
detail.abstract: The environmental sustainability of healthcare is gaining increasing attention in healthcare systems internationally, including steps to reduce the environmental impact of medicines. Patients and carers have a potential role in this, but little is known about the extent to which they are interested in the environmental impact of their medicines. This research aimed to fill this gap by evaluating perspectives from patients and carers on medicines sustainability as well as pharmacy staff experiences regarding patients' and carers’ interest in this area.,Semi-structured interviews were carried out with patients, carers and pharmacy staff who were purposively sampled in three NHS hospital organisations in England. Interviews were transcribed verbatim and subjected to inductive thematic analysis ,Sixty-five people took part: 32 pharmacy staff and 33 patients/carers across the three organisations. While themes showed a range of views and behaviours promoting medicines sustainability, interview data also suggested that people had thought less about medicines sustainability than other environmentally conscious behaviours. Barriers included lack of awareness and discussion in consultation, lack of accessible safe means of disposal, lack of confidence in availability of further supplies of medicines, and concerns about cost. Another theme was the competing priority of acute severe illness.,To promote more medicines sustainability related behaviours, further means of raising awareness outside of medicines consultations need to be employed and more accessible systems for the safe disposal of medicines are required, alongside measures to ensure that patients and carers have confidence in the reliability and continuity of medicine supply.

title: The Operational Value of Forecasting: Bridging Statistical Accuracy and Decision Utility in Healthcare Operations
affiliations: Cardiff University - Cardiff Business School, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Operational Value of Forecasting: Bridging Statistical Accuracy and Decision Utility in Healthcare Operations
detail.abstract: Accurate demand forecasting is central to healthcare operations, yet the relationship between forecast accuracy and operational utility is neither direct nor well understood. Traditional error metrics measure statistical error in isolation, without capturing the downstream consequences that matter for decisions.This study examines how forecasting accuracy translates into staffing performance in emergency departments by embedding 11 forecasting methods — including statistical, machine learning, deep learning, hybrid, and benchmark approaches — into a staffing optimisation framework applied to real-world emergency department arrival data. Rather than evaluating forecasts in isolation, we assess their operational value through staffing-relevant outcomes: daily staffing imbalance and the frequency of overstaffing and understaffing days.Our results show that models performing similarly on standard error metrics can generate substantially different staffing consequences once embedded in an optimisation framework. More specifically, forecast bias — measured by mean error (ME) — emerges as the primary driver of staffing misalignment. Models with lower bias consistently produce fewer staffing mismatches, even when competing methods achieve comparable RMSE or MAE. Crucially, forecasts that systematically over- or underestimate demand can generate substantial operational disruption despite acceptable aggregate error scores. These findings suggest that what matters for staffing decisions is not how large errors are on average, but their direction and how they interact with the structure of the optimisation model.This study contributes to the predict-and-optimise literature by demonstrating that forecast evaluation must extend beyond statistical error metrics to decision utility. It provides actionable guidance for emergency department managers and offers a generalisable evaluation framework applicable to any setting where forecasts feed into discrete operational decisions. All data, forecasting code, and the optimisation framework are made publicly available to support reproducibility and wider adoption.

detail.title: In-House Innovation Rivalry

keywords: Favoritism toward the status quo JEL Classifications: D82

detail.abstract: This paper develops a model in which headquarters (HQ) improves an existing product while an autonomous R&D unit explores an innovative alternative with breakthrough potential through experiments. We show that the two project-development activities are strategic substitutes when it is easy to improve the existing product, and strategic complements when it is difficult. This contrast arises because the R&D unit is more tempted to stop experimentation after unfavorable versus favorable early evidence across these environments. When the existing product is hard to improve, a prisoner’s dilemma arises in which both projects are underdeveloped. One solution is for HQ to adopt a “hands-on” approach, actively monitoring and incentivizing the R&D unit to prevent premature termination of the experiment. Interestingly, a biased evaluation system that favors HQ’s status quo, albeit inducing incorrect project selection in equilibrium, can outperform the hands-on approach by exploiting strategic complementarity between the rivalry.

detail.abstract:
The Predictive Quality Intelligence Framework (PQIF) is a field-deployable technical architecture designed to address a specific operational gap documented in quality engineering practice on large-scale industrial programs: existing quality management tools identify technical deviations, cost-escalation precursors, and execution-stage risk only after those conditions have already been embedded into approved expenditures, change orders, or corrective-action backlogs. The architecture combines physical sensing at the point of measurement, edge inference, multi-method predictive analytics, and closed-loop decision workflows to detect and govern these conditions while they are still reversible.

The paper documents the full technical architecture of PQIF, covering the Physical Intelligence Architecture (PIA) at the sensing layer, the five-layer operational reference stack, and the Predictive Quality Engine (PQE). The PQE integrates adaptive statistical process control, machine-learning anomaly detection, supervised fault classification, and LSTM-based Remaining Useful Life (RUL) estimation, all unified by a Bayesian risk-scoring layer. Also covered is the Autonomous Evaluation Capability (AEC), a hybrid deterministic-plus-stochastic inference system that supports continuous unattended quality-condition evaluation while keeping every critical intervention behind a human authorization gate.

A fourth module, the Cost Escalation Intelligence Module (CEIM), establishes quantitative linkage between in-process quality deviation patterns and cost escalation trajectories in federally funded infrastructure programs, providing contracting authorities with a statistically grounded early-warning capability that does not currently exist in commercial quality tooling. The framework aligns with NIST AI RMF 1.0 (2023), NIST CSF 2.0 (2024), NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, ISA/IEC 62443-3-3, and CISA Critical Infrastructure Sector guidance.

title: THE 7P LEADERSHIP FRAMEWORK Aligning the Inner and Outer Worlds of Leadership

detail.title: THE 7P LEADERSHIP FRAMEWORK Aligning the Inner and Outer Worlds of Leadership
detail.abstract: This article makes four theoretical contributions, each directed at a specific dimension of why leadership failure persists at the rate it does. First, it introduces alignment-between a leader's inner world and the outer world they face-as the central mechanism by which leadership effectiveness is produced or destroyed. Failure is not random and it is not primarily a competency deficit. It is the predictable consequence of misalignment that went undetected until the outer world made it visible as a result. Second, the framework challenges a foundational assumption in authentic leadership theory: that the inner world, once known, serves as a stable anchor. The 7P Framework argues instead that the inner world itself can drift-that a leader's Persuasions, the foundational worldview through which every situation is read and every judgment is made, can quietly grow out of alignment with a changing reality, making the inner world a source of failure rather than a corrective to it. Third, the framework extends the organizational purpose literature by arguing that organizational purpose is only as strong as the personal purpose clarity underneath it. Leaders who have not examined who they are being at the foundational level are borrowing purpose rather than leading from it-and borrowed purpose does not hold when the situation demands everything a leader has. Fourth, the framework introduces the people value proposition as a construct that operates at the individual leadership relationship level, below the reach of institutional talent management frameworks, connecting directly to Herzberg's motivator tier-the level at which genuine followership is built, and the level at which its absence first signals that failure is on its way.

title: Short-Term Vacation Rentals and Local Demand: Spatial Spillover Effects in Foot Traffic
affiliations: Arizona State University (ASU) - W.P. Carey School of Business, Arizona State University - W.P. Carey School of Business and Arizona State University

detail.title: Short-Term Vacation Rentals and Local Demand: Spatial Spillover Effects in Foot Traffic
detail.abstract: Short-term vacation rental (STVR) platforms such as Airbnb and Vrbo have transformed how demand is distributed across local economies, yet it remains unclear whether and how such activity translates into realized demand for nearby businesses. Existing research primarily examines aggregate or sector-level outcomes, offering limited insight into how platform-induced demand is manifested at the establishment level. This study addresses this gap by examining the impact of STVR occupancy on customer arrivals at proximate business establishments. Leveraging a novel dataset that links property-level STVR activity to establishment-level foot traffic across multiple service sectors, we employ a stacked Difference-in-Differences (stacked DiD) design to identify the causal effect of new STVR occupancy. The results show that new STVR occupancy increases local establishment visits by 1.4% on average, with the positive spillover effect strengthening as occupancy duration increases. However, the treatment effect diminishes with higher nearby occupancy concentration, more active days available for rental, larger maximum allowed guest capacities, and greater distance between listings and businesses. The beneficial effect appears immediately and is overall consistently observed across multiple industries, geographic regions, and seasonal variations. By offering a more holistic account of how STVR activity affects local service systems, this study extends prior research beyond aggregate outcomes to capture how platform-induced demand materializes at the establishment level. More broadly, the findings contribute to the literature on platform externalities by showing that such effects are shaped by spatial and operational constraints, highlighting the importance of demand allocation and local context in determining how platform activity translates into economic and operational outcomes.

detail.abstract: In today's rapidly evolving global economy, job stress has emerged as a more pervasive issue than ever before. Conventional perspectives often link job stress primarily to work-related conditions, yet underexplore the significant role of non-work dimensions. Personal life conditions are central to individuals' identities and often spill over into their professional domains. Recognising the profound impact of these interconnected domains on job stress is essential. Addressing this gap, the present study examines the influence of personal and familial factors on job stress. Data were collected from 140 banking professionals in Sri Lanka using a structured survey questionnaire. The responses were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) to test the hypotheses. The results indicate that the majority of employees experience a high level of job stress. Further, Individual Well-being, Personality Traits, and Domestic Support respectively emerged as key contributors, which collectively explained approximately 33% of the variance in their level of job stress. These insights support employees, HR managers, policymakers, and researchers in advancing occupational health and performance.
