detail.abstract: India's digital financial inclusion architecture has expanded through Jan Dhan accounts, Aadhaar-linked identification, mobile connectivity, e-payment systems, UPI-enabled transactions, fintech platforms, welfare digitisation and emerging blockchain-oriented public-sector initiatives. Yet the empirical and policy problem is no longer access alone. The decisive question is whether access is converted into productive credit use, livelihood assets, real capabilities, transparent welfare delivery and durable resilience among low-income households. This working paper synthesises a connected research programme on urban poverty, social welfare schemes, microcredit, fintech adoption, technology acceptance, JAM-linked e-payments, blockchain governance, capability expansion, entrepreneurship, digital market access and two earlier SSRN working papers on Punjab policy imperatives and digital capabilities in Indian slums. It proposes the Digital Poverty Alleviation Stack (DPAS), a layered capability-conversion framework explaining how digital financial inclusion becomes poverty reduction only when seven conditions operate together: access rails, user acceptance, productive credit discipline, capability conversion, community compensation, governance trust and market-access conversion. The synthesis advances three arguments. First, digital finance is poverty-reducing only when it strengthens transaction reliability and redirects credit towards productive livelihood use. Second, capability conversion is the missing bridge between financial inclusion and poverty alleviation; households benefit when digital access expands education, enterprise agency, asset formation, market participation and decision-making power. Third, governance and social structures matter as much as technology. Policy support, digital literacy, trusted networks, women's peer groups, transparent welfare systems and responsible lending safeguards determine whether fintech empowers vulnerable households or exposes them to debt traps, exclusion, fraud and algorithmic risk. The paper contributes a theory-ready framework, evidence matrix, implementation architecture and future research agenda for scholars, policymakers, fintech firms, microfinance institutions, urban planners, NGOs and development agencies.

title: Corporate Governance Speech and the First Amendment
affiliations: George Mason University - Antonin Scalia Law School and University of Illinois College of Law (deceased)

detail.title: Corporate Governance Speech and the First Amendment

keywords: Central Hudson Gas & Elec. Corp. v. Public Serv. Comm'n

detail.abstract:
The federal government regulates what corporations and their agents can say about many aspects of corporate governance. It controls communications to existing shareholders in proxy statements during director elections, communications to securities markets in filed documents and press releases, and communications concerning the purchase and sale of a corporation's own securities and those of other companies. Because this is a broad category of speech that affects economically significant activities, the issue of whether and to what extent the First Amendment applies is crucial. Thus, the appropriate scope of the commercial speech doctrine, which provides that “commercial” speech is entitled to a lower level of protection than “political” speech, must be considered. The commercial-political distinction, however, is difficult to make because much conventional commercial advertising, such as “corporate image” advertisements, has political implications. The distinction is particularly troubling as applied to corporate governance speech. Communications by corporate managers to shareholders often have many of the same characteristics as speech by politicians to their constituents.

In light of the theoretical foundations of the commercial speech doctrine, at least one category of corporate governance speech-proxy speech-should be characterized as political speech and therefore, subject to the highest level of First Amendment protection. Regulation of proxy speech, like that of the most clearly political speech, can serve the interests of legislators and bureaucrats by decreasing electoral constraints on their conduct in office, thereby increasing political agency costs. Moreover, because participants in corporate elections receive only a small portion of the benefits of their speech, and each speaker must bear a disproportionate share of regulatory costs, the costs imposed by proxy regulation can have a significant negative impact on the amount of such speech. Finally, it is unlikely that government regulators can improve on the highly efficient markets in which proxy speech occurs.

A lower level of First Amendment protection is appropriate for nonproxy securities-related speech. Nevertheless, federal regulation of this speech may be unconstitutional. First, because such speech resembles political speech in important respects, it should be placed in a hybrid category rather than being treated as ordinary advertising. Second, even under the lowest commercial speech standard, particularly under recent Supreme Court decisions that have clarified that standard, much federal securities regulation goes further than is reasonably necessary to protect the regulatory interest at stake.

It is not only the federal disclosure standards themselves that raise First Amendment problems, but also the fact that these obligations impose mandatory rules that cannot be avoided without significantly changing the structure of the transaction. Federal regulation of corporate governance speech goes against the grain of most corporate law, which recognizes that corporations are fundamentally contractual relationships. Consistent with this contractual theory of the corporation, most corporate law is enabling either in the literal sense of default rules or in the substantive sense that unfavorable laws can be avoided by choosing the incorporating jurisdiction. Such default rules do not raise First Amendment problems—the restrictions are basically voluntary and, because they are disciplined by market forces, presumptively reasonable. Mandatory federal regulation of corporate governance speech, however, is not entitled to a similar presumption because the unfavorable laws cannot be avoided by choosing another jurisdiction. Moreover, federal regulation that turns corporate elections into political contests should be subject to the higher degree of First Amendment protection accorded speech in political campaigns rather than the lower degree of protection accorded speech in commercial transactions.

title: Staffing under Taylor's Law: A Unifying Framework for Bridging Square-root and Linear Safety Rules
affiliations: , School of Data Science, Fudan University, HKUST and Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST)

detail.title: Staffing under Taylor's Law: A Unifying Framework for Bridging Square-root and Linear Safety Rules
detail.abstract: Staffing rules are an essential management tool in service industries for meeting target service levels. The square-root safety rule, based on the Poisson arrival assumption, has been commonly used. However, empirical findings suggest that arrivals often exhibit "over-dispersion", meaning that the variance exceeds the mean. In this paper, we develop a new doubly stochastic Poisson process model that captures two key features of over-dispersed arrivals: (i) Taylor's law, which links the variance to the mean through a power-law relationship, and (ii) temporal correlation decay, where the correlation between arrival counts in disjoint time intervals decreases as the time gap grows. Using this model, we study how over-dispersion affects staffing and derive a closed-form staffing formula to ensure a desired service level. Our formula shows that the safety level grows as a power of the nominal load. The exponent lies between 1/2 (the square-root safety rule) and 1 (the linear safety rule). It depends on the degree of over-dispersion, and it implies that Taylor's law is the dominant factor in determining staffing levels in heavy traffic. Extensive numerical experiments with both simulated and real arrival data show that our model and staffing rules significantly outperform various alternatives.

title: The Egiazarian Model of Sports League Development: A Systemic Framework for Emerging Markets

detail.title: The Egiazarian Model of Sports League Development: A Systemic Framework for Emerging Markets
detail.abstract: The development of professional sports leagues in emerging markets is structurally constrained by institutional fragmentation, inconsistent competition frameworks, underdeveloped commercialization strategies, and limited international integration. Although existing literature has examined isolated aspects of sports systems-such as governance, elite sport policy, or commercialization-a unified, systemic framework for league development remains absent. This paper introduces the Egiazarian Model of Sports League Development, a comprehensive systems-theory-based framework that integrates six interdependent structural pillars: (1) governance and institutional design, (2) competition structure and sporting integrity, (3) financial and commercial framework, (4) stakeholder alignment and partnerships, (5) media, branding, and fan engagement, and (6) international integration and recognition. The model is supported by a qualitative conceptual methodology that combines systems analysis, comparative institutional review, secondary global data from FIFA, the World Bank, and the IOC, and applied observations from real-world league development. A detailed case study of the Armenian Hockey League demonstrates the model's practical applicability and validation. The findings indicate that sustainable sports systems emerge not from isolated interventions but from coordinated structural alignment across all pillars and six sequential development stages. The Egiazarian Model offers both theoretical novelty and actionable guidance for policymakers, federation leaders, investors, and sports organizations operating in emerging markets.

title: Citizenship and Jurisdiction: Reclaiming the Constitutional Line

detail.title: Citizenship and Jurisdiction: Reclaiming the Constitutional Line

detail.abstract:
This Article reexamines the Citizenship Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment by focusing on the phrase "subject to the jurisdiction thereof." Modern interpretation often treats that condition as coextensive with territorial birth, subject to narrow exceptions. This reading, while familiar, is not compelled by the text. 

Drawing on the structure of the Citizenship Clause, the Reconstruction debates, and the Supreme Court's decisions in Elk v. Wilkins and United States v. Wong Kim Ark, this Article argues that "jurisdiction" has been under-read. Across these materials, jurisdiction extends beyond mere presence and incorporates concepts of allegiance, political subjection, and the relationship between the individual and the sovereign. 

A close reading of Wong Kim Ark shows that its broad language is embedded in a structure tying birthright citizenship to birth within the territory "in the allegiance and under the protection" of the United States. The modern rule depends on treating that formulation as self-sufficient, rather than as part of a larger constitutional condition. 

This Article does not seek to unsettle settled expectations or revisit prior recognition of citizenship. It instead clarifies the Citizenship Clause going forward. If  "jurisdiction" is to retain independent meaning under the Fourteenth Amendment, it must be treated as a condition that requires demonstration, not assumption.

title: The Hidden Data Advantage: Strategy, Ai & Decision Intelligence For Modern Businesses

detail.title: The Hidden Data Advantage: Strategy, Ai & Decision Intelligence For Modern Businesses
detail.abstract: This paper examines how organizations can improve decision-making by effectively utilizing both visible and hidden data. While most businesses rely on structured and readily available information, a significant portion of valuable data remains underutilized across functions. The study introduces a practical approach to identifying, integrating, and analyzing hidden data, supported by the application of artificial intelligence techniques. It also highlights key barriers such as data silos, technological limitations, and skill gaps. The paper concludes that organizations adopting a structured and data-driven approach can enhance decision quality, improve operational efficiency, and achieve measurable business outcomes.

title: Urban Science Beyond Samples: Up-to-Date Street Network Models and Indicators for Every Urban Area in the World
affiliations: University of Southern California - Sol Price School of Public Policy

detail.title: Urban Science Beyond Samples: Up-to-Date Street Network Models and Indicators for Every Urban Area in the World
detail.abstract: Urban planners need up-to-date, global, and consistent street network models and indicators to measure resilience and performance, model accessibility, and target local quality-of-life interventions. This article presents up-to-date street network models and indicators for every urban area in the world. It uses 2025 urban area boundaries from the Global Human Settlement Layer, allowing users to join these data to hundreds of other urban attributes. Its workflow ingests 180 million OpenStreetMap nodes and 360 million OpenStreetMap edges across 10,351 urban areas in 189 countries. The code, models, and indicators are publicly available for reuse. These resources unlock worldwide urban street network science beyond samples as well as local analyses in under-resourced regions where models and indicators are otherwise less-accessible.

title: Youth Development as the Foundation of Sustainable Sports Systems

detail.title: Youth Development as the Foundation of Sustainable Sports Systems
detail.abstract: The long-term sustainability of professional sports leagues and broader sports ecosystems in emerging markets depends critically on the existence of structured youth development pathways. Although professional leagues, media visibility, and commercialization often receive primary attention in sports development strategies, these elements cannot generate durable outcomes without a stable grassroots foundation. This paper conceptualizes youth development as a core structural pillar within systemic sports frameworks, particularly the Egiazarian Model of Sports League Development. Drawing on systems theory and comparative institutional analysis, the study identifies five key determinants of effective youth development: access and early entry, affordability and inclusion, coaching quality, retention and clear developmental pathways, and institutional alignment. It further examines the central role of clubs and community integration in emerging-market contexts. Empirical observations from hockey league development illustrate how integrated youth systems create athlete pipelines, enhance league sustainability, and support generational continuity. The paper contributes to sports management theory by repositioning youth development from a peripheral activity to a foundational structural component and offers practical recommendations for policymakers, federations, and league developers seeking scalable, resilient sports systems.

title: OpenMPSC: An Open Dataset of Michigan Public Service Commission Regulatory Proceedings

detail.title: OpenMPSC: An Open Dataset of Michigan Public Service Commission Regulatory Proceedings
detail.abstract: State public utility commissions regulate electricity, natural gas, and telecommunications for hundreds of millions of Americans, yet the documentary record of their proceedings remains fragmented and largely inaccessible to researchers. We introduce OpenMPSC, an open, structured, and continuously updated dataset of regulatory proceedings from the Michigan Public Service Commission (MPSC) spanning 1987-2026. The dataset comprises approximately 6,100 cases, 165,000 filings, 12,700 orders, 12,300 public comments, 2,600 hearings, and 12,300 party records, together with 3.8 million PDF pages (150 GB) and full text extracted from 3.1 million of those pages. Filings are classified into a 12-category, 86-subcategory regulatory taxonomy using an LLM pipeline. The dataset and a public REST API are available at https://openmpsc.com.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the application of automated Nesting to digital furniture manufacturing in the United States. Nesting-the computational optimization of two-dimensional part placement on raw material panels prior to CNC cutting-is classified as NP-Hard in Computational Geometry and requires heuristic or meta-heuristic algorithms in practice. The study reviews and compares two dominant strategies: First Fit Decreasing (FFD), a deterministic greedy heuristic suited to regular geometries, and Genetic Algorithms (GA), a population-based meta-heuristic capable of handling complex, irregular shapes under the anisotropy constraints inherent to woodbased materials. The technical pipeline connecting CAD design files to CNC execution via .NET middleware and G-Code generation is described as a six-stage framework (Figure 1), along with the mathematical formulation of the waste minimization objective and the role of the No-Fit Polygon (NFP) in enforcing geometric feasibility. Efficiency metrics drawn from peer-reviewed literature indicate that automated Nesting achieves material utilization rates of 88-92%, compared to 70-75% under traditional linear cutting methods, representing a waste reduction of 15-25% per production cycle and a production time reduction of approximately 35%. These gains are situated within the structural challenges of U.S. furniture manufacturing: a sector with 70% import dependency, an accelerating skilled-labor shortage, and low rates of digital adoption. The paper argues that automated Nesting is not merely an operational efficiency tool but a strategic instrument for strengthening domestic manufacturing competitiveness, reducing material waste, and contributing to supply chain resilience.

title: Collaborate or compete? The impact of strategic framing on employee ideas
affiliations: , Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Management and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)

detail.title: Collaborate or compete? The impact of strategic framing on employee ideas

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study received ethics clearance the Institutional Review Board at Columbia University [IRB Protocol #:AAAU8456].

detail.abstract: How does framing strategy around competition versus collaboration affect employee idea generation? We conduct a field experiment with 317 employees across 15 ventures in Latin America to assess the causal impact of strategic framing on employee contributions. Employees were randomly assigned to view either a competitively or collaboratively framed version of their firm's strategy statement. Those in the competitive framing condition generate approximately 14% fewer ideas and report lower psychological safety. However, competitive framing simultaneously increases the executive-rated novelty of submitted ideas by approximately 12%. The novelty effect is concentrated among firms without existing competitive orientation, suggesting that novel frames challenge existing mental models and redirect attention toward differentiation. While prior research has documented how strategic framing affects external stakeholders, such as investors and job candidates, we show that the same framing may induce novelty but at the expense of quantity of ideas among current employees. Firms based in emerging markets may be especially prone to such a novelty discount, as collaboration becomes necessary to navigate uncertain and institutionally fragmented environments.

title: 1/r³ Limits in NV-Center Biomagnetic Sensing: Helical Drone Swarms and EMP-Hardened Beacons for Rescue and Detection

detail.title: 1/r³ Limits in NV-Center Biomagnetic Sensing: Helical Drone Swarms and EMP-Hardened Beacons for Rescue and Detection

keywords: Magnetic Dipole Limit JEL Classification: O33 (Technological Change)

detail.abstract: Public reports of the classified 'Ghost Murmur' system have sparked significant interest in long-range quantum magnetometry for heartbeat detection at operationally relevant distances. This paper provides a rigorous, first-principles analysis of Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centre physics in diamond-including decoherence mechanisms and fabrication pathways-and formally derives the 1/r³ dipole field limitation that renders single-platform claims at 40 km physically implausible. Correcting an error in earlier circulated analyses, the cardiac magnetic moment is m ≈ 2.5 × 10 ⁷ A•m², yielding a required integration time of 10³ seconds at 40 km-approximately 20 orders of magnitude beyond the age of the universe, not 8 as sometimes cited. To bridge this fundamental gap, we propose a practical hybrid architecture: a helical/spiral-in drone swarm with stepwise altitude reduction and adaptive noise rejection (σ_eff ≈ 0.75 pT/√Hz for a 24-UAV formation), combined with a low-cost skin-embedded beacon protected by EMP-hardened Faraday shielding (nickel-copper ripstop or graphene/MXene composites). This hybrid system replicates Ghost Murmur-class capabilities at 100-1,000× lower cost while providing friend-or-foe encrypted identification-a critical capability absent from purely passive biomagnetic sensing. Dual-use applications span pilot rescue, border infiltration detection, miner rescue, and humanitarian operations.

title: Going Overseas: FDI Decisions and Supply-Chain Integration

detail.title: Going Overseas: FDI Decisions and Supply-Chain Integration
detail.abstract: Can outward FDI draw host economies into the investing country's supply network? This paper studies Chinese investment abroad and treats FDI not only as a movement of capital, but also as a potential channel through which sourcing relationships are reorganized. I link Chinese investment events to sector-level trade flows and firm-level production networks. At the sector level, I compare host-country supplier industries before and after Chinese investment enters their downstream customer industries, excluding same-sector Chinese investment from the exposure measure. Upstream sectors exposed to downstream Chinese investment in this way increase the quantity share of imports sourced from Greater China by 1.44 percentage points, with no evidence of differential pretrends. At the firm level, I distinguish direct supplier connections from broader network embedding. Investment recipients become more directly connected to Greater China suppliers. Beyond this direct channel, even after excluding recipients' own Greater China suppliers, their surrounding supplier neighborhoods become more China-linked: a standardized measure of indirect China-linked supplier exposure rises by 0.17-0.21 control-pre-period standard deviations during the first three post-investment years. Comparable exposure to non-Greater-China foreign suppliers does not increase significantly. The evidence indicates that Chinese outward FDI is followed by a measurable reorientation of host-country supply networks toward China. Outward investment can therefore operate as a channel of supply-chain integration, extending China-linked sourcing beyond the boundaries of the investing affiliate itself and creating a potential source of demand for home-country upstream suppliers.

detail.title: Social Science Research Network (SSRN) Article Relationship between Project Management Maturity Levels (PMML) and the Overall Success Rate of Construction Projects, as Measured by Key Performance Indicators Author
detail.abstract: The construction sector in Trinidad and Tobago has historically played a pivotal role in national development, substantially contributing to economic growth. In response, numerous organizations have begun to implement Project Management Maturity Models (PMMMs) as a strategic initiative to enhance project execution and operational efficiency. Although the international literature affirms the positive impact of Project Management Maturity Levels (PMMLs) on project outcomes, empirical research specific to the Trinidad and Tobago construction sector remains scarce. This study evaluates the influence of PMMLs on the success of construction projects in Trinidad and Tobago by examining the relationships between maturity levels and critical success indicators, including budget compliance, schedule adherence, and output quality. Utilizing a quantitative methodology and a non-experimental correlational research design, the study conducted statistical analyses to determine the nature and strength of associations between PMML and project success metrics. The results demonstrate a strong, statistically significant positive correlation between elevated PMMLs and enhanced project outcomes, thereby affirming the value of project management maturity within the local construction industry. These findings address a notable knowledge gap in the Caribbean context and provide empirical support for strategic planning, policy development, and capacity-building efforts in the sector. By contributing to both the theoretical and practical discourse on project management in developing economies, this research offers actionable recommendations aimed at advancing project management maturity and optimizing project delivery in Trinidad and Tobago.

title: Female Entrepreneurship and Economic Resilience in Sudan: An Analysis of Informal Sector Adaptation Strategies in Conflict-Affected Areas

detail.title: Female Entrepreneurship and Economic Resilience in Sudan: An Analysis of Informal Sector Adaptation Strategies in Conflict-Affected Areas
detail.abstract: This study analyses the resilience mechanisms developed by female entrepreneurs in Sudan's informal sector using World Bank ISES data. The findings reveal a systemic revenue disadvantage of 46% for female entrepreneurs relative to their male counterparts. The principal contribution lies in identifying a paradoxical protective effect: in areas of moderate conflict exposure, the gender gap narrows to 10%, whereas under high exposure it widens to 87%. This non-linearity reveals adaptive capacities specific to women that partially offset structural disadvantages under moderate crisis intensity. 23% of the performance gap is explained by differences in endowments, while 77% reflects persistent structural barriers. Sectoral analysis shows that female entrepreneurs predominate in food trade and develop adaptation strategies distinct from those of their male counterparts. These findings challenge uniform vulnerability models applied to women in conflict settings and point toward reconstruction policies that target endowment constraints while capitalising on female entrepreneurs' revealed adaptive capacities.

title: Terrain-Aware Multi-Objective Optimization of Campus Wireless Backhaul Links Using Link-Budget Modeling and Radio Mobile Validation
affiliations: African Leadership University, , African Leadership University and African Leadership University

detail.title: Terrain-Aware Multi-Objective Optimization of Campus Wireless Backhaul Links Using Link-Budget Modeling and Radio Mobile Validation
detail.abstract: Campus backhaul links are often planned from linkbudget calculations and then adjusted after terrain simulation. This paper develops a terrain-aware planning model that selects antenna height and antenna gain for a point-to-point 5.8 GHz campus backhaul link while satisfying received-signal and fademargin constraints. The model combines free-space path loss with terrain and statistical correction terms calibrated from Radio Mobile simulations. A 30-scenario matrix was generated for a 7.159 km link between the Nyarugenge and Remera campus sites using antenna heights from 5 m to 30 m and antenna gains from 10 dBi to 24 dBi. The Radio Mobile results show fade margins from 0.23 dB to 53.68 dB, with 23 of 30 scenarios satisfying a 20 dB margin and 13 of 30 satisfying a 30 dB margin. Free-space path loss alone produced a received-signal MAE of 8.337 dB against Radio Mobile. Adding an average terrain/statistical correction reduced the MAE to 6.574 dB, while a height-calibrated correction reduced the MAE to 0.043 dB. Under the normalized deployment-burden objective used in this study, the minimum-cost feasible design is 5 m and 10 dBi for a 20 dB margin, and 5 m and 16 dBi for a 30 dB margin. The results show that antenna height should not be selected by a monotonic "higher is better" rule when the terrain obstruction term changes with height.

detail.abstract: Frameworks for assessing national space development have focused on technological milestones such as satellite capabilities and launch capacity. While useful for tracking hardware progression, these instruments do not capture the governance conditions that shape whether developing countries can sustain their space activities. This article proposes an adapted framework that integrates governance milestones into the Space Technology Ladder (STL) developed by Wood and Weigel. The instrument identifies nineteen milestones across five development levels (Nascent, Low, Regular, Medium, and High), incorporating items such as national space policy adoption, the institutional nature of the space agency, regional organization membership, publicprivate partnerships, and governance architecture. Applied to Peru as an illustrative case, selected for its known combination of technical achievements and governance deficits, the framework produces a diagnostic profile in which eight of nineteen milestones have been achieved, with gaps concentrated in governance and institutional categories rather than technological ones. Peru has acquired satellite capabilities, deployed university nanosatellites, maintained cooperation agreements with NASA and APSCO, and signed the Artemis Accords in 2024, without having adopted a national space policy or a governance framework. The adapted framework makes this asymmetry between technical capacity and institutional architecture visible for the Peruvian case. The application demonstrates the instrument's operability; its discriminatory power across diverse configurations, and its utility differential relative to existing technology-only frameworks, remains to be established through comparative application to cases where outcomes are less predictable. The instrument is offered as a working tool for researchers and policymakers, subject to the limitations described in Sections 3.4 and 5.3.

detail.abstract: People in interdependent cultures explain others’ behavior less through internal traits and more through external situations than those in independent cultures. Criminal justice research suggests that this should make people more lenient. They should blame less, punish less, support rehabilitation more, and perceive offenders to have less risk to reoffend. Yet, studies across cultures contradict this theoretical prediction. We address this contradiction by proposing the idea that culture shapes how much people consider the causal attribution of offenders’ behaviors. Across two studies, compared to those from independent cultures (i.e., European Americans), participants from interdependent cultures (i.e., Asians/Asian Americans) relied less on their causal attribution when determining blame (Studies 1A, 1B), as well as punishment, support for rehabilitation, and likelihood of offenders’ re-offense (Studies 2A, 2B). Next, we asked people how well they thought offenders could reintegrate into society after they had received punishment and underwent rehabilitation (Study 3). Causal attributions for offenders’ past crimes still had more influence on European Americans’ reintegration predictions than those of Asians/Asian Americans. Together, these studies suggest that culture shapes not just the types of attributions people make, but also how much they consider those attributions when they decide how to respond to criminal acts.

title: Leadership Failure in Crisis Management: A Comparative Analytical Reading of the Models of the King and Pharaoh in the Qurʼanic Narrative

detail.title: Leadership Failure in Crisis Management: A Comparative Analytical Reading of the Models of the King and Pharaoh in the Qurʼanic Narrative
detail.abstract: Leadership failure in crisis management has been extensively studied in contemporary management literature, yet the Qurʼanic narrative remains largely underutilised as an analytical framework for understanding this phenomenon. This study addresses that gap by conducting a systematic comparative analysis of two contrasting Qurʼanic leadership models — the King in the story of Joseph (PBUH) and Pharaoh in the story of Moses (PBUH) — to identify the structural determinants of leadership success and failure in critical contexts. Drawing on a deductive qualitative method, the study applies a five-element analytical framework derived from crisis management and leadership literature: cognitive flexibility, information openness, institutional delegation, de-escalation management, and emotional intelligence. The analysis reveals that leadership failure in crisis management is fundamentally rooted in the leader’s internal disposition rather than external circumstances, and that the Qurʼanic narrative offers a rich and methodologically rigorous source for developing leadership models that integrate classical Islamic scholarship with contemporary management theory.

detail.abstract: The "value-action gap" occurs when people do not act according to their own deep beliefs. This remains a major challenge in the social sciences. Older theories often judge this behavior as hypocritical. Because of this, they struggle to explain why people change their actions so quickly under sudden, real-world stress. This paper introduces the Integrated Contextual Practice Theory (ICPT), a new socio-mathematical model. Instead of labeling people as moral failures, ICPT views the individual as an "Adaptive Agent." The theory uses simple math to show that our everyday behavior is a constant balance between what we want inside-our Habitus, Values, and Identity-and the real-world barriers we face outside, called Contextual Stress. All of these actions are guided by society's rules, which the model calls the Cultural Governor. A key update in this model is the addition of a small stability parameter"𝜺" (Epsilon). This ensures the math formula works perfectly and remains stable even in completely stress-free situations. By combining social theory with clear mathematical logic, ICPT offers a shared, practical tool for predicting how human beings adapt to different situations.

title: Exploring the link between human capital, R&D, productivity, and their growth effects in emerging and developing economies

detail.title: Exploring the link between human capital, R&D, productivity, and their growth effects in emerging and developing economies
detail.abstract: This study investigates the interlinkages between human capital, R&D investment, productivity, and economic growth in a panel of 60 emerging and developing economies from 2000 to 2023. Employing a system-GMM estimator to address endogeneity, the study finds that the direct effects of R&D and industrial productivity on growth are often weak or negative. However, the analysis reveals crucial complementarity roles. Human capital acts as a pivotal moderator, unlocking the growth potential of innovation. The positive and significant interaction terms show that R&D expenditure boosts economic performance only when coupled with a skilled workforce. This moderating effect is particularly pronounced in medium-and high-tech industries, which possess a stronger absorptive capacity. The findings highlight that pursuing innovation or industrial upgrading in isolation yields limited returns. For emerging and developing economies, strategic policy must therefore integrate targeted investments in skill development with technology adoption incentives to foster sustainable, productivity-driven growth.

title: Institutional Quality and Human Capital as Drivers of Non-Linear Export Complexity: Global Evidence

detail.title: Institutional Quality and Human Capital as Drivers of Non-Linear Export Complexity: Global Evidence
detail.abstract: This study investigates the dynamic synergy between human capital, institutional quality and trade openness, and the impact of this synergy on export complexity across a global panel of 143 countries from 1998 to 2024. Utilising a two-step GMM estimator, the research identifies a substitution effect between labour quality and governance. Initial level estimations revealed an explosive path-dependency in trade structures (autoregressive coefficient of 1.14), necessitating a pivot to a firstdifference estimation. The preferred model indicates that while human capital and institutions independently drive complexity growth, their interaction is negative and significant, suggesting that education initially acts a a bypass mechanism for industrial sophistication in weak-institution economies. Furthermore, while long-term debt levels may signal structural stagnation, the level of capital access is found to be a significant catalyst for complexity expansion. These findings offer a new framework for improving economic complexity efficiently in developing economies.

title: The Tech-Driven Revolution in India’s Food Industry: Digital Dining

detail.title: The Tech-Driven Revolution in India’s Food Industry: Digital Dining
detail.abstract: The Indian food industry, a vital pillar of the nation’s economy and cultural heritage, is experiencing a trans- formative shift propelled by rapid technological advancements. From precision agriculture to blockchain-enabled supply chains and the explosive growth of online food delivery platforms, tech- nology has redefined the production, processing, distribution, and consumption of food. This paper provides an in-depth analysis of these technological impacts, exploring their implications across agriculture, food processing, delivery systems, and consumer behavior. By synthesizing data from industry reports, academic studies, and recent trends, we highlight key opportunities, such as enhanced productivity and market access, alongside challenges, including economic disparities and environmental concerns. Our findings underscore the need for inclusive and sustainable strategies to ensure that technological advancements benefit all stakeholders in India’s dynamic food ecosystem.

title: Below the Waterline: Employer Attrition, Survivorship Bias, and the Systemic Failure to Detect Regional Economic Deterioration

detail.title: Below the Waterline: Employer Attrition, Survivorship Bias, and the Systemic Failure to Detect Regional Economic Deterioration

declarations.ethicsApproval: All data was QECW data available to the public.

detail.abstract: Using Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) payroll records — a census-level administrative instrument covering approximately 97 percent of all civilian wage and salary employment — this paper documents a multi-year employer attrition cycle in the 13-county Alamo Workforce Development Area (WDA) of South Central Texas that proceeded undetected by conventional monitoring systems through at least the third quarter of 2025. Private-sector employer establishments peaked at 61,634 in Q3 2023 and declined to 60,808 by Q3 2025, a net loss of 826 employers over eight quarters. Year-over-year private-sector employment growth decelerated from +22,733 (Q3 2022 to Q3 2023) to +6,409 (Q3 2023 to Q3 2024) to +30 (Q3 2024 to Q3 2025) — a 99.9 percent deceleration in net job creation. We identify three compounding failure modes: (1) survivorship bias in firm-level and aggregate wage metrics that systematically signals health as weaker employers exit; (2) the NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee's structural incapacity to detect sub-state regional contractions; and (3) confirmation bias in regional economic governance that converts isolated positive indicators into narrative certainty. We further address the methodological requirement to exclude government employment from private-sector assessments in military-anchor economies. The paper proposes a QCEW-based early warning framework for regional workforce governance bodies.

detail.abstract: Public debate around the 2028 U.S. presidential election has begun well before formal campaign launches. Using an initial unstructured dataset of online messages drawn from multiple social media platforms, this report structures such online data to examine early narrative themes in the pre-campaign environment. The analysis finds a fragmented discourse landscape characterized by dispersed Democratic candidate attention, elevated negative sentiment, and issue conversations that appear to remain unsettled rather than consolidating around a single dominant theme. Several prominent political figures receive recurring attention, but most candidates do not possess durable narrative ownership at this stage perhaps with the exception of Marco Rubio who appears to be seen positively for his foreign affairs experience The findings suggest that the current timeframe may be less useful for forecasting outcomes than for documenting the early stories that may later scale into key campaign themes. While social media data should not be treated as representative of the broader electorate, it offers a glimpse into how political identities, criticisms, and issue associations are beginning to form across a broad spectrum of social media platforms in advance of official candidacies.

detail.title: Task Efficiency and Signaling in the Age of GenAI: Effort Reallocation and Firm Value Effects
detail.abstract: I study how Generative AI (GenAI) reshapes effort allocation and firm value by affecting both productivity and signaling. Using developer-level data from U.S. public firms' open-source projects, I construct a novel AI exposure measure and exploit GitHub Copilot's launch as a shock. I find that GenAI increases coding productivity for senior developers while juniors create more valuable projects. This is consistent with seniors capturing productivity gains while career-concerned juniors shift toward creative work that better signals ability, as GenAI erodes coding's signaling value. Changes in signaling incentives are reflected in project selection, programming language choices, and job moves across firms. Stock market reactions to GitHub Copilot's launch show that non-innovative firms with senior-heavy teams, where signaling incentives align with productivity goals, benefit most. A multitask signaling model rationalizes these patterns. These findings shed new light on the dual role of GenAI as a productivity tool and a force reshaping labor market signaling.

title: The Sisyphean Pursuit of Evidence for Poverty Traps

detail.title: The Sisyphean Pursuit of Evidence for Poverty Traps

publicationDetails.detailsText: Buffett Institute Global Poverty Research Lab Working Paper (forthcoming)
publicationDetails.journalName: Global Poverty Research Lab, Kellogg School of Management, Northwestern University Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Much of development economics, both micro and macro, posits theories and explores the empirics of poverty traps. A common theory centers around asset-threshold poverty traps in which marginal returns to capital increase sharply over a certain threshold and financial markets are incomplete. This combination leads households above this threshold to prosper while those below continuously fall back, trapped in poverty. Yet in economics, as best as we can tell, far more papers assume such thresholds than empirically demonstrate them. In a key recent exception, Balboni et al. (2022) (hereinafter "BBBGH") argues that data from Bangladesh identifies clear evidence of such a threshold at slightly above the cost of a cow for recent recipients of a big push transfer program. We apply this analysis to data from seven other similar programs in low-income countries and find no evidence of an asset-threshold poverty trap. We then return to BBBGH and argue that their data do not support the identification of a poverty trap, with the point of disagreement being a log-transformation challenge and a potential geographic confound. In long-term representative rural panel data from Bangladesh and Ghana we find no evidence of divergence away from any particular threshold. While the threshold theory is undoubtedly true for some households, we argue that the pursuit of clear evidence of an asset-threshold poverty trap for a broad population is likely an aspirational goal rendered unachievable by the intersection of a multitude of possible mechanisms as well as heterogeneous agents.

title: More Access, More Competition: UnintendedConsequences of Public Education Expansion in China

detail.title: More Access, More Competition: UnintendedConsequences of Public Education Expansion in China
detail.abstract: Although education fever is widespread across East Asia, the role of public education investment in intensifying this fever remains underexamined.  By leveraging the staggered rollout of county-level free senior high school education pilots in China, we find that this major expansion of public education increased the number of registrations at private tutoring centers by about 20% and doubled household spending on tutoring. Using administrative night-light data and elite university admission records, we show that the effect is driven by more intensive competition for scarce top-tier college placements rather than by declining public school quality. The response is strongest in regions with greater income inequality and lower elite university admission rates, but substantially weaker in areas with better outside options, such as higher local employment rates. Our findings suggest that expanding access to senior high school alone may exacerbate educational arms races, underscoring the need for complementary policies that reduce income disparities and broaden postsecondary opportunities.

title: AI Adoption and Firm-Level Wage Structures: Evidence from China

detail.abstract: This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) adoption affects firm-level wage outcomes in Chinese listed firms. Using 30,560 firm-year observations from 2011 to 2023, we measure AI adoption through textual analysis of annual reports. We find that AI adoption is positively associated with both employee wages and management wages. The results remain robust across instrumental variable estimation, propensity score matching, a policy-based difference-indifferences design, and alternative AI measures. We further show that workforce restructuring is an important channel: AI adoption increases the share of highly educated employees while reducing reliance on lower-educated workers. In addition, the wage effect is stronger in non-state-owned enterprises, and AI adoption weakens pay-for-performance sensitivity.

detail.abstract:
This study examines the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on employment and workforce dynamics in business organizations. With rapid advancements in AI technologies, organizations are increasingly adopting automation, machine learning, and data-driven systems to enhance efficiency and productivity. The research explores how AI influences job creation, job displacement, and the transformation of skill requirements within the workforce.
The study is based on secondary data collected from research articles, industry reports, and case studies. Findings indicate that while AI leads to the automation of routine and repetitive tasks, resulting in job displacement in certain sectors, it also creates new employment opportunities in areas such as data analysis, AI development, and digital management. The study concludes that AI has a dual impact on employment, posing challenges as well as opportunities. Organizations and employees must focus on reskilling and upskilling to adapt to the changing technological landscape.

detail.abstract:
Scholarship on post-AGI behavioral outcomes has grown substantially, yet predictions about human motivation, social organization, and meaning-making under conditions of material abundance remain largely ungrounded in empirical observation. Where behavioral assumptions appear — concerning purposelessness, motivational collapse, and social disintegration following labor displacement — they derive from theoretical frameworks that treat employment as the primary source of human meaning, without recourse to populations that approximate post-scarcity conditions. This paper identifies and argues for a methodological correction.

We propose that homogeneous affluent residential communities — neighborhoods where material security constitutes a normalized intergenerational baseline, social comparison operates primarily within the peer group, and survival pressure is functionally absent from daily psychological life — represent an underutilized and methodologically defensible behavioral proxy for post-AGI research. We develop four criteria for proxy population validity and demonstrate that homogeneous affluent communities satisfy them more completely than existing alternatives. We specify the behavioral domains for which the proxy is valid — intrinsic motivation under material security, status competition dynamics when material scarcity is removed as a differentiator, social hierarchy formation within homogeneous peer groups, meaning-making outside employment, and identity formation under security — and those for which it is not, including political behavior, family formation, religiosity, and transition dynamics.

Drawing on community psychology research, upper-class social cognition literature, aspiration and goal research, residential segregation evidence, and Self-Determination Theory, we examine what this proxy reveals within the specified domains. Dominant post-AGI behavioral concerns are systematically miscalibrated within these domains. Social complexity increases, intrinsic motivation persists and redirects toward non-material goals, and status competition organizes around competence, cultural capital, and physical challenge rather than material accumulation. Transition risk concentrates in workers with exclusively work-anchored identities — not the workforce broadly.

We conclude with a research agenda for empirically grounding post-AGI behavioral prediction. This paper was developed through human-AI collaboration between a researcher and Claude, an AI assistant developed by Anthropic.

detail.abstract: Global governance scholarship has documented a persistent institutional deficit in the international architecture for AI oversight, produced by the fragmentation of existing multilateral initiatives and the absence of proven design precedents. This article advances a structural argument: the institutional architecture capable of addressing that deficit has operated across fourteen centuries and within a $3.88 trillion contemporary asset class, transmitted into Western governance foundations through the Iberian Peninsula and currently active in global Islamic capital markets. Drawing on comparative institutional analysis and the theory of multiplex world order, the article maps the structural equivalence between Islamic institutional governance and the accountability architecture that AI oversight demands. That equivalence is architectural rather than analogical: Islamic institutional design integrates tiered oversight, auditability, prohibition frameworks, human dignity as a binding constraint, and the distribution of productive gains within a single architecture-the design properties that Western AI governance frameworks are currently attempting to construct modularly and without precedent. The article traces the transmission of this architecture through Al-Andalus into Western institutional foundations, maps its operational presence in contemporary Islamic capital markets, and derives implications for development finance institutions, sovereign capital allocators, and policymakers implementing the EU Artificial Intelligence Act. The findings contribute to debates on non-Western governance architectures, regime complexity, and the institutional design of international regulatory order.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence has rapidly transitioned from experimental capability to operational infrastructure, outpacing the evolution of governance systems, workforce development, and institutional control. While AI delivers measurable gains in task-level productivity, emerging evidence points to uneven value realization, increased system dependency, and erosion of human expertise.

This paper introduces the sovereignty crisis, a systemic condition in which institutions improve output faster than they preserve the capacity to understand, audit, and govern AI-mediated operations. Drawing on interdisciplinary evidence, the paper develops a framework linking workforce atrophy, cognitive overreliance, technical vulnerability, and infrastructure concentration into a unified model of systemic risk.

The analysis argues that these dynamics produce conditions of accelerated fragility, where performance improvements mask declining institutional control. To address this, the paper proposes the Red Switch Mandate, a governance framework emphasizing human mastery, auditability, constrained privilege, diversified dependencies, and operational fallback.

The central claim is that the defining tradeoff of the agentic era is not innovation versus regulation, but speed versus sovereignty.

detail.abstract: Article 14 of the EU AI Act makes human oversight a core requirement for high-risk AI systems. Article 26 requires deployers to assign that oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training, authority, and support (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689). The legal structure is therefore clear on one point: compliant oversight is not merely a technical feature of the system; it is also a human operating condition. What remains under-specified is how organizations should determine whether the people assigned to that function can actually perform it under real operating conditions. This paper argues that a practical gap exists between architectural compliance and human governance capability. Existing governance instruments are increasingly robust at documenting policies, controls, instructions for use, logging, and escalation pathways. They are much weaker at assessing whether the human layer of oversight can resist automation bias, sustain judgment under cognitive load, and activate accountability boundaries in time (NIST, 2023; OECD, 2024). The result is a plausible mode of failure in which an organization may appear procedurally prepared while remaining operationally fragile. The paper makes four contributions. First, it clarifies the legal structure created by Articles 14 and 26 and distinguishes the provider's design obligations from the deployer's operational obligations.

detail.abstract: Non-consensual intimate image sharing (NCIIS), colloquially termed 'revenge porn,' has emerged as one of the most pervasive and damaging forms of technology-facilitated gender-based violence in Nepal during the 2023-2025 period. Nepal's rapid digital transformation-characterized by internet penetration rising from 67.8% in 2023 to an estimated 72.3% in 2024 and the proliferation of smartphones and social media platforms-has created fertile ground for image-based abuse. Yet the country's legal architecture remains structurally ill-equipped to address this harm with the specificity and urgency it demands. This paper presents a comprehensive, mixed-method review of NCIIS in Nepal, drawing upon police cybercrime statistics, judicial records, media reports, civil society documentation, and secondary academic literature. It analyzes patterns in perpetration and victimization, documents at least four illustrative cases from 2022-2025, evaluates the adequacy of the Electronic Transaction Act 2008 and ancillary legislation, and benchmarks Nepal's legal response against those of India, the United Kingdom, Australia, the United States, and the Philippines. Findings indicate that reported NCIIS cases increased by approximately 49% between fiscal years 2022-23 and 2023-24, with women and girls aged 15-35 constituting over 85% of identified victims. Structural barriers-including social stigma, victim-blaming cultures, digital illiteracy among law-enforcement officers, and the transnational nature of online platforms-significantly impede justice. The paper concludes with targeted policy recommendations including the enactment of a standalone NCIIS statute, the establishment of a dedicated cybercrime victimsupport unit, mandatory platform-cooperation protocols, and curriculum-embedded digital-safety education.

title: Nudging the Digital Mind -A Dual-Process Perspective on Nudge Susceptibility in LLM-Based GUI Agents Behaviour

detail.title: Nudging the Digital Mind -A Dual-Process Perspective on Nudge Susceptibility in LLM-Based GUI Agents Behaviour
detail.abstract: This study investigates whether LLM-based GUI agents, autonomous systems that navigate graphical user interfaces, exhibit susceptibility to behavioural interventions. Using a randomized online shopping experiment with 1,800 agents across three leading LLMs, we examine agents' responses to digital automatic (Type 1) and reflective (Type 2) nudges under two LLM reasoning configurations by drawing on System 1-(low reasoning) and System 2-like (high reasoning) thinking in Dual-Process Theory. Results show that agents across all LLMs are systematically influenced by both nudge types and that reasoning capacity moderates these effects in opposing directions. Specifically, higher reasoning reduced susceptibility to automatic default nudges while simultaneously increasing responsiveness to reflective social influence nudges, though the strength of these effects varied substantially across models. These findings demonstrate that improved reasoning does not render agents more robust; rather, it shifts their vulnerability from automatic to reflective influences. The study highlights the behavioural nature of agentic AI and underscores the need for safeguards in digital choice environments.

title: The Geometry of Decision-Making in DAOs: An Information-Theoretic Mapping of Consensus and Disagreement in Decentralized Token Voting

detail.title: The Geometry of Decision-Making in DAOs: An Information-Theoretic Mapping of Consensus and Disagreement in Decentralized Token Voting
detail.abstract: Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) are digital communities that make collective decisions by voting on blockchain communication-systems, amongst other coordination media. "Token voting" is intended to, on the one hand, efficiently synthesize individuals' limited information toward collective intelligence, on the other, it is presented as an inclusive approach to the governance of organizations-allowing any member with tokens to voice their opinions. In this latter sense, DAO decision-making is described as 'decentralized governance,' a misnomer, as most DAOs exhibit extreme centralization in token allocation. Yet, this paper finds value in DAO's collective decision-making intentions: the core blockchain infrastructure, when paired with a DAO's collective voting, produces an immutable, peerproduced ledger of group decision-making. Much empirical and theoretical attention has focused on consensus, understood as the majority-supported outcome of a vote. This paper argues that such a focus is incomplete. Consensus is often treated as a signal of a collective's certainty in a chosen outcome, yet this certainty depends on the structure of the decision space. The same majority share can imply different levels of certainty depending on the number of available options and how support is distributed across non-winning alternatives. As such, collective decisions cannot be evaluated by majority size alone, but must be understood relative to how a community allocates support across the full set of choices. To this end, this paper proposes the Rényi family of entropy-based measures, along with several derived metrics, as tools to map the topology of consensus and disagreement. It applies these metrics to voting data from 277 DAOs to signal (1) whether dissenting opinions converge into coordinated blocks of collective opposition or disperse pluralistically across the decision space, and (2) the effective number of choices and relative weight of substantively engaged alternatives within the choice set. The former heuristic qualifies the type of disagreement to ask "did disagreement converge into viable minority alternatives?" The latter heuristic quantifies the number of options that were seriously considered, and to what degree?" Altogether, this paper contributes a formal information-theoretic framework for representing the topology of collective decision-making through the distribution of support across all alternatives. It provides heuristics that treat a community's decision-making quality as a design question and enables majority outcomes to be interpreted relative to how support is distributed across the full set of choices, rather than in isolation.

detail.abstract: A representative long-haul 1,000 km terrestrial quantum key distribution (QKD) deployment over commercial fibre infrastructure has demonstrated the feasibility of extended-range quantum-secure links. However, such systems rely on trusted-node repeaters and legacy optical transport equipment, creating exploitable attack surfaces for sophisticated adversaries. The Human Indemnity Quantum Transmission Framework™ (HIQTF™) is the first comprehensive defence-grade architecture that simultaneously defeats honey traps, social engineering, NFC/EM side-channels, firmware backdoors, and trusted-node compromises while preserving 100% of the secret key rate. HIQTF™ migrates the baseline system to Twin-Field QKD (TF-QKD) with an orbital untrusted "Charlie" relay, augmented by PRF-deterministic basis selection and behavioural AI. This paper provides (1) detailed TF-QKD equations and 1,000 km-class deployment parameters, (2) adversarial threat analysis, (3) direct architecture comparison, (4) an orbital relay benchmark and deployment roadmap, and (5) a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for immediate integration. title: Intelligence and Authority: On the Structural Behavior of Decision Systems in High-Stakes Environments

detail.title: Intelligence and Authority: On the Structural Behavior of Decision Systems in High-Stakes Environments
detail.abstract:
The expansion of data infrastructure and artificial intelligence has transformed how organizations generate and apply intelligence. These developments are commonly framed as improvements in analytical capability and decision quality. This paper argues that such framing is incomplete. The central issue is not the production of intelligence, but its structural behavior within systems where authority, accountability, and autonomy must remain distributed.

Rather than treating intelligence as a neutral enhancement, the paper conceptualizes it as an architectural force that reshapes decision environments. Drawing on socio-technical systems theory, high-reliability organization research, and emerging work in AI governance, it introduces Non-Intrusive Intelligence as a behavioral category describing systems whose outputs remain structurally decoupled from enforcement, prescription, and authority reallocation.

Using high-stakes environments such as healthcare systems as a reference context, the analysis examines how intelligence systems, when embedded without constraint, can generate unintended shifts in authority and coordination. The contribution is conceptual. It reframes intelligence as a structural phenomenon and outlines the boundary conditions under which it can operate without transforming into a governing mechanism.

detail.abstract: This paper reexamines student acquisition on the basis of CRM and the theory of the sales pipeline in private education where the flows of enquiry are abundant but the conversions are dubious. The study speaks to a persistent ineffectiveness wherein institutions fail to translate growing numbers of student enquiries stemming from digital mediums into confirmed enrollments. It has been highlighted that there is no existing framework which connects principles of pipelineing with the processes of admission in education, model can be designed to bridge the gap with a structure and data. The study takes up a quantitative approach and relies on secondary data of institutional CRM and admission dataset taking a sample size of 200+. By employing regression, funnel, and correlation analyses, this study systematically evaluates stage-wise transitions across the enquiry, qualification, follow-up, offer, and enrollment pipeline. The study reveals that traditional systems that respond late and lack proper communication see higher drop-offs at early and mid-stage. On the other hand, implementing CRM-driven practices like lead scoring, autofollow-ups, and real-time tracking greatly improves all pipeline stages. The empirical evidence shows a striking enhancement in overall conversion efficiency as the enrolment rate under the CRM model exceeds 50%, while the traditional model reflects a figure of around 22%. The follow up and offer stages see the greatest benefit, where the structured and timely engagement plays a critical role in impacting the choice of students. The reduced drop-off rates only further indicate that student acquisition is better managed effectively as a pipeline than being an administrative process. This is the writing on the study under Avinash Pillai and al whose study repositioning of enquiry management as a strategic and revenue generating function. Moreover, it also contains performance metrics for continuous monitoring and improvement. Finally, this study contributes both theoretically and practically. This proposal extends the existing framework of CRM theory to the sphere of higher education, creating a framework amenable to scale for better enrollment results. Essentially, the research concludes that when guided by the structure, data, and intent, the journey from enquiry to enrollment is not chance but one articulated with clarity and precision for the journey that can stay permanent.

detail.abstract: The growing trend of artificial intelligence (AI) being implemented in various fields-including regulated, safety-critical, and those involving significant amounts of datahas produced an acute need for large quantities of quality test data. Use of actual data from production for testing purposes is typically restricted due to factors such as data privacy laws, protection of intellectual property rights, ethical considerations, and the potential operational risks associated with the use of sensitive data. As an alternative, there have been numerous attempts to produce synthetic data; however, previous methods used to create synthetic data are generally unable to provide contextually relevant data, dynamically adapt to changing system requirements, and be semantically aligned with the characteristics of actual data in use in the system. This paper proposes the development of an Agentic AI-based framework for the generation of synthetic test data, which includes autonomous, goal-oriented AI agents that collaborate to develop, produce, validate, and improve the synthetic test data. In contrast to the static nature of typical synthetic data generation methods (including rule-based methodologies and generative algorithms), this proposed framework utilizes multiple agent types-including schema agents, constraint agents, scenario agents, adversarial agents, and validation agents-to dynamically evaluate the structure and content of the synthetic test data generated during each iteration. This allows for the continuous evolution of the test data based on changes in the system under test, regulatory restrictions, and the behavior of the models. Through empirical testing and analysis across both enterprise and AI-enabled system testing environments, the proposed framework was able to demonstrate better test data coverage, higher defect discovery rates, stronger privacy guarantees, and increased robustness testing when compared to the conventional synthetic data generation pipelines. Therefore, the proposed method represents a viable option for generating synthetic test data at scale while providing auditable and regulatory compliance solutions for AIdriven systems.

title: CaliFusion-CNN: A Confidence-Calibrated Multimodal Framework for Robust Cancer Diagnosis Under Dataset Shift

detail.title: CaliFusion-CNN: A Confidence-Calibrated Multimodal Framework for Robust Cancer Diagnosis Under Dataset Shift
detail.abstract: Objective: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems for cancer diagnosis often demonstrate strong performance in controlled settings but fail to generalize reliably in real-world clinical environments due to data heterogeneity, dataset shift, and lack of uncertainty awareness. This study proposes a framework designed to address these limitations by aligning diagnostic predictions with clinically meaningful decision-making.Methods: We introduce CaliFusion-CNN, a multimodal deep learning framework that integrates imaging data with structured clinical variables through modality-specific encoders and a fusion mechanism. The framework incorporates post-hoc confidence calibration to provide reliable probability estimates and supports threshold-based decision logic. Evaluation was conducted across heterogeneous datasets and experimental conditions using clinically relevant metrics, including sensitivity, specificity, AUROC, predictive values, and agreement measures.  Results: The multimodal configuration demonstrated improved diagnostic performance compared to single-modality approaches, achieving higher sensitivity, specificity, and agreement with reference annotations. Confidence calibration enhanced predictive reliability by reducing overconfident errors and improving performance at clinically relevant operating points. Sensitivity analysis showed that multimodal integration and calibration contributed to robustness under variable data conditions, including reduced image quality and incomplete clinical information.  Conclusion: CaliFusion-CNN provides a clinically aligned framework for cancer diagnosis that integrates multimodal learning with uncertainty-aware inference and deployment-oriented evaluation. By emphasizing reliability, interpretability, and robustness to dataset shift, the proposed approach supports more trustworthy and actionable AI-assisted decision-making in oncology.
